title: Games Industry News Roundup- September 22nd, 2026
content:
Here at Tabletop Battles, we know that it’s hard to keep track of all the news happening all the time in the games industry. So much is always going on, all over the place, all the time. With games of all sorts, and their related media, being an informed gamer can feel impossible some days. 

That's why every week, we help you stay in the know by rounding up five of the biggest recent stories in the gaming and gaming-related pop culture sphere in the Games Industry News Roundup. Our trusty news boy, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson, is right here at the very real, and cool TTB newsdesk with the scoop.

Mammoth-Sized Updates for Kings of War

Credit: Mantic Games

We’re joined this week by Cytoplasm to start us off with some big updates to Kings of War, and yes, the pun was intended.

Cytoplasm: The biggest Kings of War event in the world, Clash of Kings UK, has just wrapped up and there have been some big reveals about what’s coming up over the next year. 

The biggest news is that the biannual releases of new books (of which we have already had two, Invasion and Fracture) will be turning to a yearly release schedule. Mantic says this will give the playtesters more time to provide feedback, but also allows them to expand the scope of each book to give rules updates to all factions rather than a select few. This will be in the form of new Command Orders, updated Unit Profiles and even a change to army construction to enable greater flexibility.

This is definitely a good move. The overall sentiment among Kings of War players that two books a year was a bit too quick. Jokes about mental aptitude aside, the real issue is that Kings of War is a long-term hobby. Every army is a long journey from start to finish, and to find out by the time that it’s finally complete that half of it needs to change does not resonate well. While the general contents of the books has been well-received, slowing it down can only help both the players enjoy what they have, and Mantic make the best update they can.

The Sheer Arrogance book, like the books before, will have a few armies that will receive particularly close attention in the form of revised army lists and new models! Twilight Kin, Northern Alliance, Abyssal Dwarfs and Xirkaali will be the focus. 

The Twilight Kin will be getting new units including some War Machines and Impaler variants. The Abyssal Dwarfs are getting new sculpts of older models, including the Overmaster on Ancient Winged Halfbreed. Even the Xirkaali, which are the newest faction to join Kings of War, are being expanded with new units like the gorilla warriors known as the Shaoquan and Yan Warrior Monks on horseback.

The most exciting update however is the new Mammoth for the Northern Alliance. Whether you think the Mammoth is a good unit or not, all can agree that this new model sets the standard for Mammoths. The best thing is, multiple factions in Kings of War have access to the Mammoth, including Ogres and Kingdoms of Men, so it’s almost like a an update for three armies rather than just the one!

Wizards Cancels Product for Upcoming Star Trek Set

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

The Universes Beyond sets released over the past few years have become the cornerstone to Magic: The Gathering’s financial success, breaking sales records and driving a wider engagement with the venerable card game. Wizards has pushed UB hard to maximize profits, with each release bringing a plethora of new releases, limited edition collectible sets, as well as big pushes for community events. In the past, Wizards has been more than happy to oversaturate the market and the brand with each new UB release, but in a rare move, it looks like with the Star trek release, we’re dialing it back rather than speeding the train up, as Wizards of the Coast announced on Monday that it would be cancelling the Star Trek Beginner Box set.

“Due to delays in production, logistics, and shipping, we will no longer be producing the Magic: The Gathering® | Star Trek™ Beginner Box,” Wizards of the Coast announced on the Magic blog page. “This product has been canceled in all regions. If you preordered a Beginner Box, contact your local game store or retailer for more information. For Magic events that planned to include the Beginner Box (like MagicCon: Atlanta), we are currently updating our plans and will share details in the future.

“No other Magic: The Gathering | Star Trek products are affected by this. We appreciate your patience and understanding.”

The set, which was set to retail at $25, contained two twenty card starter decks, with one themed for Starfleet and the other for Klingons, designed to be played against one another for learning games. Once players felt comfortable, the set also included eight half decks of twenty cards each that could be mixed and matched with one another for players to kickstart their Magic collections with and dive into full games. Alongside the two hundred cards included in the set, the beginner box would also include playmats and learn to play guides for each player, as well as two spindown tokens for tracking life. 

Wizards gave no further elaboration as to what exactly the logistic, production, and shipping issues with the Star Trek set are that would necessitate cancelling the Beginner Box, though the company has been recently facing a plethora of supply chain issues with its releases. This includes the recent delays to the upcoming Reality Fractures set, which was set to release in early October, though now several products have been delayed and will have very limited availability at launch, particularly in North America. 

Focus Entertainment Fires Back at Toxic Community Members with Legal Action

Credit: Focus Entertainment

It’s no secret that online video game communities can produce some of the most wretched, despicable posters ever to troll through the alleys of cyberspace, with focused harassment campaigns against video game developers becoming a grave concern in the modern industry. Focus Entertainment has had enough though, and in a recent statement stated their intention to pursue legal action against members of their fan communities that are engaging in online harassment towards their team. 

Focus released a statement on their social media page addressing the toxic actions taken by unnamed members of their online fan community, condemning their actions and expressing their right to take legal action in their team's defense. The statement in full reads that, “Today we’d like to remind everyone about the rules of conduct of this community.”

“We expect you to contribute to an environment where everyone feels welcome, respected, and included, be it fellow community members, moderators, dev teams, or Focus staff. Focus staff have sadly seen their share of toxic messages over the past years, but a recent escalation has led Focus Entertainment to file formal legal complaints against players directly threatening team members.”

“Our networks and hubs are about passion, not hatred. We are proud of our team and will not tolerate violent or sexist comments. We reserve the right to take all necessary legal action to protect our staff. Thanks for your attention.”

Focus, wisely, did not share any further details as to the nature of the harassment against their team, or who was targeted by the attacks.

While most reasonable folks would read this, nod and say, “Hey, good on them for standing up for their team”, there were others who attacked the statement as “a violation of the free speech of community members.” Focus responded to this by writing that, “Racism, sexism, death threats, harassment of any kind: are NOT free speech, we will never tolerate any of this.”

One particularly tenacious jerk even tried to reference badly interpreted United States law regarding freedom of speech to defend the harassment, to which Focus Entertainment simply responded, “We’re French.”

Focus Entertainment has not put out any further official statement regarding the legal action at time of writing.

Hyperlight Drifter Studio Faces Possible Collapse After Publishing Deal Falls Through

Credit: Heart Machine

Hyperlight Drifter was one of the most visually striking indie games of its time, mixing retro graphics with a bright, surrealist artstyle that quickly made the game a classic. At the time, the future looked incredibly bright for the studio behind the game, Heart Machine. The future is here now, and rather than being filled with hope and possibility, it is instead deeply grim. Heart Machine studios announced that due to a recent publishing deal for one of its titles falling through the studio faces imminent closure, having already been forced to lay off the majority of its staff to continue to operate in any capacity.

Alx Preston, the studio head at Heart Machine, shared the news on his LinkedIn. 

“We had been working on an unannounced title, funded by a publisher. This week, they decided to no longer move forward with it. Without this key income for the studio, any other immediate prospects or other funds, nearly everyone at the studio had to be laid off. It's devastating.”

Preston elaborates that the studio will do everything it can for those employees that were let go, as well as offering to help with networking and finding new jobs for those affected. As for the future of Heart Machine, Preston writes that he does not know what it will take for the studio to survive, but that the remaining staff will do everything they can to stay afloat. 

Despite the success of Hyperlight Drifter thrusting Heart Machine to the international gaming stage, the studio has struggled to make lightning strike twice, having gone through multiple rounds of layoffs since October 2025.

Heart Machine voluntarily recognized a workers union formed by 13 of its employees earlier this year, and at time of writing it is unknown if any of those workers who were let go were a part of this union.

Bungie Announces Plans to Return Vaulted Content Back to Destiny 2

Credit: Bungie

It’s been a real bad year for Bungie, having launched Marathon to far less success than initially hoped and laying off nearly its entire Destiny team as they told its dedicated player base that it would be closing the doors on Destiny for good following one last update earlier this year. In a welcome bit of good news though, it looks like Destiny might not be so dead after all, as the new leadership team for Destiny announced last week that all of the previously locked away raids and story content are being released from the vault, alongside teasing work on future destiny titles. 

The blog post and associated video statement from Bungie come from two of the newest members of studio leadership, studio head Poria Torken and Marathon’s general manager Josh Deane. In the statement, Torken and Deane recognize the frustration and disappointment that fans have felt with bungie regarding many of the company’s recent decisions, highlighting a need for the company to hold itself accountable and do better in the future. 

“Bungie has been creating games for over 30 years and we have welcomed the communities that have formed around them,” the pair write on the blog post. “Over the last few years, we lost sight of that, and there have been real consequences. We lost trust, we lost incredible colleagues, and we lost sight of what we should be prioritizing most, our players. As a new leadership team, we must own that.”

Alongside general updates to Marathon to expand its PvE content and build a more widely engaging game, the widespread outcry and sunsetting Destiny spurned the team at Bungie to open the doors back on the franchise. Alongside planning for new content in the future for Destiny, the team is focusing on one of the most prominent criticisms of the game: the expansive amount of old content that has been cut from the game. 

Bungie plans to release these old raids and storylines out from the content vault for the Destiny 2 player base to enjoy, letting old and new players alike experience the history and story of the game. The development team does note though that this process will take time, since the old content will need to be modernized and balanced to work with the current version of Destiny 2.

“When we look to the future of Destiny all up this restoration is the first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve,” the team writes. “We’ll have more details on our unvaulting efforts in the coming months, and we’re very excited to share more about our vision to celebrate Destiny’s legacy and build its future with you all as soon as we can.”

title: Turn Order: Making Paper Minis for TTRPGs with a Silhouette Portrait Digital Cutting Machine
content:
What Is a Silhouette Portrait 4?

The Silhouette Portrait 4 is a computer controlled cutting machine designed to work with paper, card, vinyl stickers, and dozens of other materials. It’s the smaller cousin of wood working routing machines and metal laser cutters that looks a bit like a home printer.

Credit www.silhouetteamerica.com

They have a variety of uses, from cutting out custom stickers or stencils, scoring card for creating 3D model nets, or for the use I’m discussing today, cutting out paper miniatures.

Paper minis designed by PrintableHeroes.com and PaperForgeMinis.com, printed by Vre'Kais

Other Brands of Cutter

Silhouette is just one brand of digital cutting machine available, Cricut is another popular brand but it has its own software and processes. This guide will focus on using a Silhouette Portrait 4 but much of the process will be similar for other brands, and should be identical for any other Silhouette model. If you want to follow along with this guide, download and install the Silhouette Studio software and follow any required registration steps.

Where to Get Paper Mini Art

For this guide I’m using art created by Printable Heroes, sort of, the miniature I'm making today was actually created by a community member from the Printable Heroes Discord server using parts of several other Printable Heroes miniatures to create something new. It’s a great community that I can’t recommend enough.

What I'm looking to print and assemble today is called a Strix, a menacing construct featured in Curse of Strahd: Reloaded which is the campaign I’m currently DMing.

Adapting Other Art

Whilst this guide uses purposefully designed paper miniature art you can make paper miniatures from any monster art you have available. I’ve made miniatures using Hero Forge for instance using images of the 3D mini from the front.

Combination of Hero Forge mini and PrintableHeroes.com art, photo by Vrekais.

There are some compromises when using art this way; if it’s art from a book or adventure it’s very rare that you’ll get a front and back profile of the monster, so your mini will probably need to have the same front and back art work (but mirrored for the other side). If you’re using a Hero Forge image it’s technically possible to get a front and back image, but it’s not trivial to make these images actually work. Perspective is crucial here; if the 3D mini’s pose or equipment extend to far forward or back from the centre vertical plane of the mini then those features will vary in size between the front and back images. This can make lining up the two images very difficult, and cause them to not precisely match up. It’s generally easier to stick with the same art for front and back but don’t let me tell you what to do!

How to Print, Cut, and Assemble Your Paper Minis

So we have our cutter, our art, and our software, let's get started actually creating the mini!

Preparing the Page

Start by creating a new project from the File Menu. This will take you to the default blank project. Here we have a few options and steps to consider.

By default the software has loaded an A4 sheet as my page; while the cutter will handle A4 reasonably well, in my experience with the machine it needs proper support otherwise the flex in the cutting mat caused by its own weight can cause an uneven cut at the designs extremities. For this reason I actually tend to print and cut my minis from a smaller A5 sheet. Let's set that up now in the panel below.

If these settings are not currently visible, they can be accessed by clicking on the Page Setup Panel button located at the top of the toolbar on the right hand side.

After setting our page size A5 we now need to tell Studio to print “registration marks”, these show us where the cutter can cut and allow the cutter to align itself with our printed design. Open the registration marks panel to configure them.

Tick “Enable Registration Marks” and configure the inset value you wish to use, this will change the usable space on the sheet. Because I’m using A5 media that is well within the range and accuracy limits of the cutter it’s pretty safe to reduce the inset of the registration marks to their minimum settings here. I would probably recommend 15mm or even 20mm if using A4 or similar sized media though. Your project should now look like this.

Now we’re ready to add some art. This guide will go step by step through doing this manually, some paper mini art providers do actually have Studio Cut files available that can skip some of this work. I don’t use them for two main reasons:

  1. I print my minis at 15mm scale; I do this so that I can fit greater distances on maps on my VTT screen.
  2. I print my minis with an attached square base. Printing minis without a base is fairly common at full scale as it saves storage space and slot bases for full scale minis are widely available. If you’re using this guide but don’t want to print with a base, you can skip those steps in my process.

Preparing the Art

Drag your .png into the Studio software. It should look something like this.

Yes, that is too big. Zoom out using the buttons at the top of the design or by holding ALT and scrolling back (towards you). I would then usually drag the mini art to the side of the project like this.

You might notice at this point the whole piece has a red line around every edge; this is normal. We will address this later on in the guide.

Clean Up and Positioning

Most paper mini art will include a square box and base drawn around the mini in the .png you download; this will need to be removed. The Strix art I’m using doesn’t have this box because it’s a “kit bash,” but I’ve included a box around it just to demonstrate how to remove it. Locate the eraser tool on the left tool bar.

Erase the box at the points it touches the mini art you want to keep.

So that your project looks something like this.

The studio software actually divides imported art up into contiguous parts, so at this point we actually now have four separate parts, the front and back of the mini, and the two box remnants on either side. We can now select and delete them but using the Select tool in the left toolbar. It should now look like this.

Before we move onto scale there’s the matter of the red line. By default when you import images into Studio, it detects the outline of the image and adds a 0mm offset cut to the art work. That is what the red line is showing. We do not want it to cut this close, so we need to change this line from red to transparent. The studio software uses coloured lines of 0pt thickness to determine the type and path of cuts to be made, because these lines are actually 0pt thick they will not be printed on the design; they only appear in the editor.

To change the line to transparent select all parts of the art (remember it’s likely to be in two parts now) and click the line colour menu located in the top left to set the line colour to transparent.

This should remove the red line you could see. Now we can move on to position and scale.

Position and Scale

Scaling Paper Minis is not an exacting science; there will always be compromises. These instructions will detail the process I use to keep my minis consistently scaled with each other, but working out what works for your own tables will take some trial and error.

On my table maps us a 15mm grid (rather than the typical 1” grid), each square representing the usual 5ft. So my minis are scaled with 15mm = 5ft roughly in mind, tending to be closer to that scale exactly the larger the monster in question actually is meant to be. For instance if I’m making a 3ft tall Halfling mini, those tend to be slightly more “heroic” in their scaling because a 9mm tall mini isn’t terribly practical on the table.

With that in mind we need to scale the Strix, it’s a large monster (taking up a 2x2 space on the grid) and I’m picturing something between 12-15 ft tall. So at my 15mm to 5ft scale that’s going to be roughly 36mm tall. Lets start by drawing a box 36mm tall to fit out mini within.

Using the Shape Tool draw a rectangle into our design as shown; its size doesn’t matter right now.

Select this rectangle and change its size using the size controls at the top of the editor. You may need to click the pad-lock icon to the right of these controls to disable ratio locking so that the numbers can be adjusted independently.

I’ve made my box 30mm wide and 36mm tall. The width is based on it being a 2x2 mini making it 2 grid squares wide. This box is just a guide though. Next we’ll need to reposition our art and scale it down. At this stage I would suggest that if there’s a large gap between the front and back art, make that gap a lot smaller now, a few mm at most. Then reduce the size of both parts together by selecting them and using either to corner anchors or by turning ratio locking back on with the padlock button and typing in a new height into the box (remembering that this number will be more than double the eventual height of the finished mini).

Grouping the separate art parts at this point will help you ensure they stay aligned with each other (available in the right click menu). Then we can drag the art within the guide rectangle so that the front part of the mini fits within it, and adjust the scale until you’re satisfied. This particular mini is going to overhang its base significantly due to its large wingspan so only the feet and body will be within the rectangle.

I’ve added a few already finished minis to my project at this point just to check that the scale fits right with minis I’ve already printed and assembled. I’d highly recommend doing this once you have a few minis made as it really helps keep everything looking right.

This is looking menacing enough compared to a Zombie and one my group's character minis.

Adding a Base

At this stage I would normally add a base to the mini. If you’re not planning to use attached bases skip this section of the guide.

My bases are square but I actually create them as two separate triangles so that the eventual mini is on the base at a 45 degree angle. I do this so that regardless of which way the mini is placed on the table no player is looking directly at a thin edge face on, they should have a pretty good view of the front or back from any cardinal side of the table. It’s not perfect, but I think it does help slightly.

There is not however a “triangle tool” so to make one has a few steps. Start with a rectangle, sized as required using the same method I showed earlier. For my needs I’m going to make a 29mm by 29mm one. It should look like this (though I’ll eventually change the outline of this to the same red, it’s black for now to help illustrate where cut lines are later in the guide).

Right now though this won’t print as it’s just a red box with 0pt thickness. We need to change that using the line colour tool, and line thickness tools in the top left.

I tend to use solid colours for my bases; using art is possible but slightly more complex if mimicking my triangular base method. The colour fill setting is directly to the left of the line colour option. I’ve gone with a deep red here as I use colour to help distinguish between friend and foe on the map.

Making it into a triangle is next. To do this we’re simply going to remove one of the vertices. First though, take a copy and paste it into the project (I’ll explain why we want this later). Then right click on one of them and click “edit points”.

Then simply click on and delete one of the corner points. You should now have this.

We can now copy and paste this triangle for the front and back half of the base, and arrange them around the mini art on the page. It should look something like this now.

I’ve brought that square we made as well, we will need this to mount the finished mini on when it’s printed.

Next we move on to tell the machine where to cut.

Cut Lines

The mini’s cut lines will usually be a few mm away from the mini itself, this avoids trying to make the machine do really really tiny cuts for details really close together. Lets select our mini art (not the base) and add a offset cut. To do this select to Offset Cut Panel from the right hand tool bar, click the “offset option” in the top left of the panel and set a distance for the cut. I’ve gone with 0.7mm. Then click Apply.

As I had both pieces of art selected, these cut lines have actually “welded” where they overlapped here. This is expected and will be the basis of where we fold the mini once printed. You can have them cut entirely separate to be lined up later but I find the folding method a bit quicker.

Note. This mini art is a kitbash, so the alignment of front and back won’t be as perfect as it would be for other minis from the printable heroes catalogue. This is expected. For the best results with modified minis, it’s sometimes best to just have the cut line trace the front art of the mini, and then copy and mirror that cut line for the back art. I’ve done that for this mini but it’s not a step usually required for most minis.

At this point there may be some cut lines contained within the mini; depending on the scale of the mini some of these might work if left in, some might cause the mini to be quite flimsy and fragile. In the case of the Strix here it would put a lot of strain on two very thin legs so I am going to remove the internal cuts. To do this we need to disconnect the cuts from each other as they are all linked by default. Select the cut line by clicking one and then right click. Select “release compound paths” and this will break up the cuts into each separate part.

You can then select all the internal cuts, and delete them.

Now we need to add cut lines for the base. It’s essentially the same process but I want it offset 0.2mm to cut close to the outline of the base. Once done the project should look like this (you might need to right click and “send to back” to see this).

Here’s the most fiddly part of my process, though. We now need to “weld” the cut lines of the base and the mini together otherwise we’ll just end up cutting the base off the mini. I’ve tended to find the easiest way to do this is actually to select everything and then use CTRL click to deselect the mini art and the base, so you should end up with JUST the cut lines selected. With only the cut lines selected, press CTRL + SHIFT + W to “weld” them; this is also available in the Object > Modify menu at the top of the screen, and technically in the right click menu but in my experience trying to right click when doing this causes you to accidentally select something else. If welded correctly the cut lines will look like this between the base and mini art.

Lastly, I’ll add a cut line to the square base offset at 0mm; this will make it slightly smaller than the base of the mini itself so that it doesn’t poke out from under it.

Scoring and Perforating Folds

This is largely optional but at this stage you could add more lines to tell the machine to score or perforate some fold lines for you, to avoid doing them manually. Which one you use will depend on which way the line is folding as the machine can’t score both sides of the sheet, only the top.

The middle fold between front and back faces can be scored using a scoring line. I’ll explain the settings for this when we get to cutting the minis out but for now draw a line through the centre and give it a distinct colour. This line will by default be 0pt wide and registered by the software as a cut line, but by giving it a different colour we can tell the machine to do something other than cut along this specific line. It should look like this.

The folds for the base however would ideally be scored on the other side of the sheet as they are going to fold the opposite way, we can’t do that. What we can do however is perforate the sheet slightly to make this folder easier. If I’m honest, this works, but it’s not as good as scoring the eventual print out by hand. For a single large mini like this I would probably do it manually, but if you’re printing dozens of zombies, it’s a massive time saver. If you are doing it, it’s the same as adding a scoring line but we’ll change it from a solid line to a dotted one, and give it a different colour. The options for this are all located in the top menu to the right of the line colour, and thickness.

It should look like this (replicated for top and bottom).

At this point I’ll change the base outline to match the base colour, it just ends up looking neater if you do this. I’d recommend at this stage clicking on the SEND mode (button top right of the screen) to check that all the lines you expect to cut are the only ones present. It should look something like this.

Now we have this all set up, it's time to print. If I wanted to have several of this mini at this point I could copy and paste all of this work several times on the sheet, this way you can make large hordes of minis like these Zombies very quickly.

Designed bu PrintableHeroes.com printed by VreKais

Printing Your Minis

Printing your minis has a few steps to consider here based on your media of choice. I print on 220gsm A5 card stock; the US system of paper weights and types is a bit more arcane though. This should be roughly equivalent to 80lb card stock, but I also know plenty of people who use 68lb matte photo paper.

If you’re using media similar to mine, especially any without a photo print coating, adjusting the brightness and saturation of your print can drastically change its quality. Heavier papers tend to absorb more ink causing the image to appear darker than intended, causing any darker details to be very hard to see. I’d suggest digging through your printer settings for the custom brightness and saturation settings, I tend to increase brightness by 10% and Saturation by 5% (at least I think these settings are in %).

And obviously if your printer has a print quality setting, set this to as high as it goes. This will adjust your printer’s resolution to highest, literally moving the paper slower to print thinner lines on each pass.

Now that we have our printed design, it's time to cut.

Cutting Your Mini Out

After all of that, we are finally at the cutting step. Remove the protective cover of your cutting sheet, and press your printed media onto the adhesive side as shown in the software (if you put it in the wrong place it will not find the registration marks).

Make sure you firmly press your design down onto the cutting sheets sticky, if it comes loose during printing the blade will just drag the sheet around rather than cut it. Line up the cutting sheet into your machine and hit the load arrow button on the machine, it should look like this when inserted.

BEFORE we get too excited though, we need to make sure all the cut settings are set correctly. This design has three different types of cut we want to do. These settings are found in the SEND mode we used earlier.

Red: A cut through the material to release the mini from the card. This will be the deepest cut we do. For the card I’m using I tend to set the blade depth to 5 and do two passes. The settings for the red lines should look like this.

Purple: This is a score line between the front and back artwork for folding the mini. I’ve found the “score” preset works just fine for this. The presets are nothing special, they just change the depth and force settings to specific values. It should look like this.

Green: This is the perforating line to help us fold the base, whilst it sounds fancy it’s actually just a cut line but because it’s dashed it will only cut on the dashed parts of the line, lifting the blade to move over the gaps. We don’t want to go all the way through for this one though so I’d reduce the depth to 2, and only do a single pass.

With all those settings checked, it’s time to press send and cut out our print. One tip I’ve found useful here is to make sure you have something supporting the print sheet on either side as when it sags it can leverage the print off the print sheet, keeping it as flat as possible mitigates this. With that all set up, hit send, and watch it go. It will scream like it’s possessed by a goblin. This is normal.

Removing Your Cut Minis from the Cutting Sheet

When finished eject your cutting sheet from the machine. I’ve found that the best way to remove the print from the sheet is actually to flip it over a peel it away slowly from above like this.

Please ignore that this photo has the design on the back of the card, I forgot a setting and didn’t want to waste the card so the corrected print is on the other side!

Sometimes when doing this the cut out design will remain on the sheet, sometimes it will come with it needing to be popped out. In either circumstance be careful not to tear any elements when it. I find using a flat knife black can help remove it from the sheet. Your cut design should look like this.

Assembling Your Mini

All that’s left to do here is to assemble them. Fold the mini along that centre line between the front and back artwork, and fold the base outsides along the perforating lines. I usually do a dry fit fold first before gluing anything, that should look like this.

Finally using some form of stick glue, something like Pritt Stick in the UK, or I believe Elmer’s in the USA, glue the front and back together, being careful to get it aligned properly and then glue the base to the square of card we had cut out as well with our mini. The finished Mini should look something like this.

And we’re done! Hope you all agree that the finished little guy looks very menacing and scary, just in time for my next Curse of Strahd Reloaded session! If you’d like to give this exact mini a go or use it as a template or guide for your own minis I’ve uploaded the studio cut file here.

title: Disney Lorcana reveals Illustrious new Evil Queen and an Iconic Cinderella for Hyperia City
content:
While Hyperia City is the next and final Lorcana set due to release this year, collectors are already peering ahead at 2027's Into the Inkdark, ancitipating the debut of the absurdly rare Illustrious cards. Limited to just 23 copies per card, publisher Ravensburger revealed the second of these Illustrious rares on Tuesday - an elegant reprint of 'The Evil Queen, Commanding Presence' from Rise of the Floodborn.

Illustrious rares will only be available in Collector Booster packs, a new product type that will debut in February 2027 with Into the Inkdark. There'll be six Illustrious rare cards per set, and each individual card will be printed with a serial number.

It's going to be a lot better for your mental wellbeing to pretend Illustrious Rares don't exist when you're opening packs - they'll be as rare as rocking horse poo. We may have to exclude them from our guide to the most expensive Lorcana cards just because they are definitely going to dominate the list, and it's going to get pretty boring just tracking six cards from each new set.

Moving to something comparatively humble, Ravensburger has revealed two Iconic rares from Hyperia City: 'Cinderella, Unintentional Icon', and 'Mickey Mouse, Best in Town'. These both have simple - but festive - art.

In gameplay terms, Cinderella looks like quite a powerful top-end card for Sapphire decks that have a way to protect her: she can Quest for three Lore, has a fairly respectable six Willpower, and if she's exhausted at the end of your turn, she lets you put a card from the top of your deck into your Inkwell exerted.

Mickey Mouse, Best in Town has been somewhat spoiled by leaks from an earlier presentation, but we now have a better picture of what his rules mean. With no Strength, four Willpower, and the ability to Quest for two lore, all for one Ink, he looks like a classic Amber card that will get you questing early at a great rate. But if he's exhausted at the end of your turn, each player gets an Ink Drop counter; these are single-use Ink counters.

While that looks like a symmetrical bonus for both players, the symmetry is actually a little broken by the mere fact that you know you'll have this advantage when you build your deck, and your opponent doesn't. But for a more structured way to take advantage, Ravensburger has revealed plenty of new cards from the set that get better when you remove Ink Drops.

1/3

If you remove an Ink drop to play the new Madam Mim, Resourceful Trickster, you get to draw two cards, and then once she's in play each time you remove an Ink Drop you draw a card; and the new Baymax, Amped Up can be shifted on top of another Baymax by removing two Ink Drops, and then lets you put the top card of your library into your Inkwell when you would gain Ink Drops in the future.

With songs and discard-pile shenanigans as the other major themes, the gameplay for Hyperia City looks very interesting, and the new chase cards are as pretty as ever. If you're a big Lorcana fan, why not show of the crown jewels in your collection in the friendly Wargamer Discord community?

title: Malifaux Fourth Edition: September Errata/FAQ
content:
When Wyrd released their July balance errata, they warned that "We will still be doing an errata on the comprehensive rules in September and release GG1 then as well." And lo, it came to pass! We have a brand spankin' new set of errata and FAQs!

Let's dive in and see what's changed and what, conspicuously, hasn't!

Errata and FAQ

Third edition had (mostly) two errata cycles per year; it would be nice to hit that cadence in Fourth!  This is more like the "second half" of the July errata, though. Let's rip off one band-aid now: there are no model changes here. Instead, this update is focused on the core rules of the game.  That doesn't mean that Wyrd thinks the game is perfectly balanced; it just means that any further adjustments to crews will come in the next wave. The changes here are still significant enough that many crews will have to rethink how they play in ways large and small.

Leave Your Mark Works Now

I thought the Leave Your Mark ruling was insane at the time and said so. Now, it's gone. You can't block your opponent from scoring Schemes like Leave Your Mark by standing on the centerline; when a Scheme measures a distance between a Marker and a point on the board, Line of Sight is no longer required, just like measuring between two Markers. Frankly it should always have worked this way, and there's no reason this had to be an errata rather than the answer to the earlier FAQ.

Take Command Doesn't Break in Smaller Formats

Take Command, the rule by which a Henchman can be promoted to Master when your Master dies, had some weird interactions with smaller formats; below 50ss, Masters only get two actions rather than three. But with Take Command, your Henchman always got three actions after being promoted, regardless of how many the Master had originally. Now if you Take Command in a format where your Master formerly had just two Actions, your Henchman only gets two... which begs the question of why you would do that.

Controlled Models Can't Discard Upgrades

This is really just closing a loop. Controlled models could never attach upgrades. Now they can't discard them either. It's rare, but it means you can't just Zoraida's Obey to make people ditch their Mimicry upgrades, or Ophelia's guns, etc.

Sorry, bog lady. We all know you were winning way too many games lately. Credit: Wyrd Games

Generated Actions Come Last

I don't know that anyone was playing this wrong, but someone must have been. Now it is more clear that, when you generate an action, it gets added to the end of the action queue. So if you already have something queued up, you do that first. This is a very rare interaction and won't come up often.

Terrain and Markers Can Overlap

The FAQ answer to "what happens if I drop a Piano on a Strategy Marker?" was very weird, and arguably didn't even match the rules text. Now it's much easier: when you make terrain (i.e. a marker with terrain traits) on top of an existing marker, they overlap. Easy peasy.

Yes... ha ha ha... YES! Credit: Wyrd Games

Now You Shuffle Your Deck in Between Flipping for Attacker and Determining Strategy and Deployment

The sole reason for this is that, because the suit of the Attacker's card determined the Strategy and the Attacker always had the highest card, you could never flip the Black Joker for the Strategy. That matters now, so they changed the rule.

You Can't Score Terrain Schemes With Terrain You Made

Fair. You shouldn't be able to Search the Area on an Underbrush marker you dropped. You know what's in that Area! You made it yourself!

Models with No Cost Always Count Their Health as Their Cost

They already did for Scheme purposes, but there are a very small number of game effects that key off of model cost as well. Now these work the way they intuitively feel like they should.

Objects on Crew Cards Are Not in Play

I think most people played it this way already, but there are a few effects that put a model or Marker on your crew card (i.e. Calypso/Beebe), and this clarifies that such objects are not in play and so don't count towards model/Marker limits.

That's it for the errata - very mild - but the FAQ adds a few new notes:

Are Slow and Summon Tokens Created When Summoning a Model Allied or Enemy?

They're friendly to the model summoned. Next question.

When Do You Remove Aura (Staggered) Tokens?

Never, unless you're told to. Pretty powerful for the few crews who have them.

your day has come, bally-hoo bucket. Credit: Wyrd Games

Can You Make a Marker Overlapping a Strategy Marker?

Yes, unless the Strategy Marker is Impassable or there's some other rule that says no (i.e. "make this marker not in base contact with any other marker").

Can You Score Reshape the Land With Markers Your Crew Makes (i.e. Pianos)?

Yes, obviously!  That's what that Scheme is for!

Is Generated Terrain Entirely Ignored When Scoring Schemes?

Not entirely. It can still block LOS and so on. You just can't choose a generated piece of terrain when scoring a Scheme that asks you to choose a piece of terrain.

Does the Smolder Trigger Give You Burning If You Didn't Already Have It?

Yes. First you resolve Burning if they have it, then you give them a new Burning regardless.

How Does Won Over Work on Winston Finnigan?

This trigger can't be controlled by enemy models. Technically this is an errata rather than an FAQ but fuck it, that would have created some mind-melting interactions, so better to leave it.

the face of a man who loves causing problems with the rules, on purpose. Credit: Wyrd Games

Can a Woe Remove Its Own Token to Activate Opportunist When It Is Targeted By an Attack?

Yeah. I mean, that's what the ability says. You remove a token from the target and it applies to any opposed duel. Go nuts.

How Does Gift of the Queen Work on Titania, Autumn Queen's Crew Card?

Now you "may" add a crow once per activation, so if your first Action is to Charge, you don't have to add the crow to your Charge movement, you can add it to your Attack (as long as you're still within 1" of the Marker). Technically another errata, but Titania can use the buff.

Can I Resolve Relish In Blood Whenever Anyone Makes An Attack That Damages Anyone Anywhere on the Board?

No. I am going to smack you with a rolled-up newspaper.

Do I Get the Free Relish In Blood Even If I Fail the TN on Nekima, Broodmother's The Strong Survive?

What is it with you Nephilim players?! NO! You do not.

If a Model Has No Cost, How Does the Rat King's Prey on the Weak Work?

We just talked about this. Use the target's health.

If a Freikorps Model Uses Adaptive Tactics and Hits the "I'm Out!" Trigger, Do You Discard the Upgrade?

Yes. It says "discard the upgrade," it doesn't matter who took the action.

Can You Use the Lament of the Cursed Trigger On Jack Daw, Ensouled's Siren's Sway Upgrade to Control a Master's Action?

Nope. You can never Obey enemy Masters, even indirectly like this.

Does the Corpse Curator's Control Graft Action Work with "New Arms?"

Yes. Technically this is an errata as it unambiguously does not work as written, but it's clearly supposed to, so yes, you can use the Corpse Curator to order a friendly model to Interact using "New Arms!" and it works.

if malifaux were a computer game this change would be patch logged as "fixed an issue with the Corpse Curator's Control Graft." Credit: Wyrd Games

How Does Catlike Reflexes Work on Kara?

The friendly model you are teleporting to must be "at elevation 2 or higher," not "on terrain." I think that was the intention but that's definitely not what it says, so this is yet another errata. I really wonder why so many of these are in the FAQ section.

Are Campaign Masters Unique by Default?

Yes.  Nice try.

So What About Strange Portal? Does That Work Still?

Yeah, don't worry about it, it works.

Faq You

So where does that leave us? Honestly, most of the lingering core-rules issues have been cleared up by this. Some shouldn't have been issues at all (cough leaveyourmark cough) but, hey, that's water under the bridge now.

There are a couple of lingering issues, such as [PLACEHOLDER]. But all in all, the rules are in a pretty solid place, so the question after this errata pass is how does GG1 shake things up? And, gentle reader, you can bet I'm going to answer that, too. Stay tuned.

title: Ascended Heroes biggest Pokémon cards are crashing in price
content:
Ascended Heroes is one of the hottest Pokémon sets of the last year, but it now seems like some of its biggest chase cards have been slightly over-hyped. In particular, the two most expensive SIR cards of Ascended Heroes: Pikachu ex (or Treekachu) and Mega Gengar ex have fallen off in recent months

While Pokémon cards usually gain value over time, these two Special Illustration Rares are notable because fans were shelling out enormous amounts for them just a couple of months after Ascended Heroes released.

The peak for both cards looks to have been around May this year, when (and I'm going by Price Charting's figures here) both were valued close to $1,300. While this doesn't hold a Litwick to the most expensive rare Pokémon cards of all time, it is an astonishing figure for a card to hit in just four months, and indicative of how Pokémon card hype has continued to grow and grow over the last five years.

A good point of comparison here is Moonbreon, a holy grail and one of the very best modern Pokémon cards on the market. While this card is valued much higher than either Gengar or Pikachu right now, its growth was much slower. It took close to three and half years - between its release in August 2021 to December 2024 - for the card to break the $1,000 barrier.

Speaking of which, Gengar and Treekachu are both plummeting back below that threshold now, with Mega Gengar ex SIR cards now consistently fetching 'just' $850 on the secondary market. Pikachu appears more in flux - with some higher $1,000 sales sticking out on TCGPlayer, but it too has mostly fallen to $800-900.

Of course, just because these cards have dropped right now that doesn't mean we can say that this is where they'll rest forever. Perhaps players will rush to 'get in on the ground floor' now these cards are looking cheaper and that will cause them to rise again. In which case, we might see them yo-yo-ing up and down for quite some time.

title: Lore to Table: Building Imperial Fists with the 11th Edition Codex
content:
The new release of the 11th edition Codex: Space Marines gave us a ton of new Detachments to play with, including a mix of generic and chapter-specific options to choose from. In this article series, we're going to be looking at different chapters and how to represent them on the table, talking about different combinations and lore-accurate forces.

I personally never loved the decision to jettison subfactions from the game. I understand why it happened; the idea of your army's rules being tied to a paint scheme definitely chafes some players and isn't ideal for competitive events. But on the other hand, I think it's common for players to associate themselves with a chapter or legion. You aren't a "Space Marines" player, you're an "Imperial Fists" player or a "Space Wolves" player. You don't want to run an army of yellow assault marines; you want cool rules for representing your Imperial Fists on the table the way the lore does.

Hence, this article series. In this series we're going to look at different ways to represent chapters and their forces on the table, using different Detachments and units. Today we're starting with the Imperial Fists. In addition to looking at current armies, we'll also play around with the occasional Legends unit where it makes sense.

What Kinds of Armies Do We Want to Build?

The Imperial Fists are traditionally the defenders of the Imperium, masters of siege warfare who build and maintain fortifications such as the Imperial Palace. They're also known for their discipline, and have had rules around that in the past. They were also among the first chapters to use Centurion warsuits in their ranks and, depending on what you believe, Centurions may have been originally intended as an exclusive unit for the chapter.

I think that there are fundamentally three or four different forces we want to look at for the Imperial Fists:

  • Trench Fighters - An army that's heavy on bulky gravis or terminator units and represents the army fighting to the last man over key defensive positions, entrenching themselves as they get dug in.
  • Bolter Discipline - An Intercessor-heavy force which focuses on the chapter's renowned use of synchronized, high-volume bolt weapon fire and tactical coordination.
  • Exploitation Force - Based on a piece of the Sternhammer Strike Force concept in the 7th edition Angels of Death book, this is a force dedicated to take advantage of enemy weaknesses and force open holes in their lines. This one's more about shooting.

This gives us three concepts to build around; a take-and-hold force heavy on Terminators and first company units, a force filled with Intercessors firing at short and medium range, and a devastator-heavy force led by Tor Garadon pounding an opponent with ranged weapons.

Imperial Fists Captain Lysander. Credit: Jack Hunter

Trench Fighters

The Core of a Sternhammer Strike Force is a force of heavily armored marines, geared up for brutal close quarters combat and grinding advances. This is where we'll want to really make use of Lysander and his Detachment, running Ceramite Sentinels as our base. On top of that we'll add Terminator Storm Force to create an army that runs 30 terminators, give or take.

This is the kind of army I love building for Take and Hold: Just running a ton of terminators to clog up the middle of the table. The concept here is pretty easy: Build around Lysander and a group of ten Terminators + Ancient, using his -1 to be hit with Cover for a unit which is -2 to be hit, has 4W each, -1 to be wounded with Stand to the End, and the option for -1 damage with Tactical Dreadnought Fortitude. 

Strike Force Lysander - Click to Expand

2,000 Points

- Spy-Skull Data Link (20)

BATTLELINE

OTHER DATASHEETS

Scout Squad (65 points)

Lieutenant with Combi-Weapon (85 points)

Land Raider Redeemer (245 points)

The core here are two big Terminator bricks, giving you 20 to work with total. That's a huge amount of beef to clog up the middle of the table - that Lysander unit is a ridiculous brick of meat to put on one or both objectives. It's difficult to shift, and having 4W models lets you sail past even 4-damage threats. And if you do come across one of those, you can give them -1 damage for 2 CP, making even those only half as useful against your unit. You can reliably tank the Lion for a couple of turns with these guys, and if you're lucky you might even get a few shots back into him.

Double Terminator bricks are a popular army trope right now in competitive play and that doesn't figure to change with the new book - 30+ wounds of T6, 2+/4++ save models are hard to chew through, and that combo pairs well with the primary mission on Take and Hold. We're just expanding on that concept here and getting more out of it with Darnath Lysander.

Here Lysander and his unit are fine to walk to midtable most games - they always count as entrenched, so you don't need to worry about when or where they come in, but the other unit won't be as fortunate. The Terminator Librarian goes in the Land Raider with his unit, and standard Terminators a better getting benefit out of both of his psychic abilities than Assault Terminators. Heavy Bolter Eradicators are just good value, and while scouts don't always have a place in the trenches, we still need fast, versatile units to help us score secondary objectives from time to time.

The Legends Version

We don't have points or Legends Datasheets yet for some of the things passing into Legends with the new release but I don't have a ton of changes I'd make here. I'd strongly consider swapping out the Eradicators, the Terminator Librarian + Terminators, and Land Raider Redeemer for Centurions and a Vindicator just to give it more 7th edition/pre-Primaris flavor if I wanted to go that route, and you're always welcome to swap Intercessors for Tactical marines in that same vein. Running 25 Terminators and a Land Raider already has enough old school feel, but I'm a sucker for Vindicators.

Imperial Fists Primaris Intercessors. Credit: Jack Hunter

Bolter Discipline

The Imperial Fists are equally known for their unparalleled skill with bolters and their ability to drown enemies in a hail of overlapping fields of coordinated fire. This is also a trait they passed down to Crimson Fists, and so I'd also consider this our "Crimson Fists" Detachment option, given there's no Pedro Kantor - though we can certainly look at him again in the Legends section.

There are no formal rules for Bolter Discipline these days, but with Gravis Linebreaker Force, Devastator Brethren, and Tacticus Firestorm Force, we can approximate a pretty good setup for making bolter marines do real damage. This army can stay mobile while putting out an absolutely punishing hail of midrange, high-AP firepower, and Tor Garadon can help them get there by pointing at targets and stripping them of cover. I initially wanted to include Boltstorm Aggressors here but they're pretty bad in the new book, so I've given Tor Garadon a unit of ten Heavy Intercessors instead.

The big downside to this list is taking on heavy armor and vehicle targets - bolters aren't great for that without some additional LETHAL HITS boosts but the good news is that you have the Annihilating Force and Storm of Fire Stratagems to help with those, giving you lethal hits and AP boosts in Devastator Doctrine, respectively. Tor Garadon is also good for that in a pinch, and anything that isn't a knight should be within reach just using sheer volume.

The Legends Version

As above, we don't have the new Legends handover yet, but my immediate thoughts here were: 1) Pedro Kantor once he finally gets his Legends Datasheet, as a way to make this Crimson Fists, and 2) Devastator Centurions. That said, I think this list gets the point across pretty well as-is, and doesn't feel like it's really missing anything from Legends at the moment. If you wanted Tactical Squads over Intercessors, I guess go for it. But they're better off as Legendary Proxies, in my opinion.

Imperial Fists Primaris Eradicators. Credit: Jack Hunter

Exploitation Force

In this final list, we're building a Devastator force. We want something that hits hard, and really makes an opponent feel our firepower in their bones. This is supposed to be the fists exploiting their ability to find weak points in enemy armor and widen those gaps to massive wounds. Here we want to take good shooting units with strong firepower, going for quality over volume, in contrast to the Bolter Discipline force.

Task Force Garadon - Click to Expand

1,990 Points

Detachment: Ceramite Centinels (2 DP)

Detachment: Gravis Linebreaker Force (1 DP)

Disposition: Take and Hold

ATTACHED UNITS

- Warlord

- Indefatigable Fortitude (20)

CHARACTERS

- Castellum Omni-Vox (15)

OTHER DATASHEETS

Repulsor Executioner (260)

Repulsor Executioner (260)

We're going to use Tor Garadon again here, because he fits into our plan of "shooting the crap out of key targets." We'll opt for the Ceramite Sentinels Detachment for the ability to re-roll wound rolls of 1, and because we're taking Garadon. We also want the Gravis Linebreaker Force Detachment again because we want to be able to move and still get +1 to hit. You've got two Impulsors here which are perfect for holding 3-man Gravis units like the Eradicators, while Tor Garadon's unit just kind of walks. It's a heavy-hitting unit with lots of OC which is capable of shrugging off attacks with Indefatigable Fortitude. Meanwhile, the Repulsor Executioners give you an anti-vehicle punch you didn't have in our Bolter Discipline list.

The Legends Version

I probably replace the RepExes with Vindicators in the Legends version. They're cheaper and do lots of damage without wasting points on the other piddly guns, and while they're not as good without oaths, they can still do some real damage. You can't really replace the Gravis marines here with Centurions without changing the whole detachment, and Devastator marines might be a good fit here but you'd need to move things around - I think if I were going that route I'd swap out Gravis Linebreaker Force for either Devastator Brethren or Ironstorm. Devastator gives you more movement and works better on things like Centurions and Devastators, while Ironstorm will benefit your vehicles more.

Imperial Fists Aggressors. Credit: Jack Hunter

Final Thoughts

There are certainly more ways to run the Imperial Fists, and as a chapter they almost certainly make use of units like Assault Intercessors, Outriders, and Bladeguard Veterans. But at the same time, when you think about the Imperial Fists, those units aren't necessarily what comes to mind and it's fun to think about how we might build armies which match that mental conception while still being reasonable to run on the tabletop.

But this is just the tip of the iceberg - we'll have more of these in the coming weeks, looking at other Chapters and how to build their armies as we become more familiar with the Codex. Likewise, what kinds of Imperial Fists armies are you building? Are there any we missed? title: D&D teases Classic dungeon Dire Maul for its World of Warcraft crossover
content:
D&D YouTubers have started to reveal details from the upcoming World of Warcraft crossover book, courtesy of a preview by Wizards of the Coast. The core of the reveals focus on the way WoW's iconic dungeons are being adapted to D&D, with Dire Maul - once an end-game dungeon in the original vanilla version of WoW - being the star of the show.

Sadly Wargamer wasn't at the preview event, so I owe a big debt to all the content creators making videos about what they've seen - I'll link out to their coverage throughout this interview, as is only polite. While we'd love to have been invited to that preview, we don't feel too snubbed - we did get to interview Dan Ayoub, Wizard of the Coast's new head of D&D, recently.

GameMasters provides some great information about the dungeons populating the book, particularly the fact that they're split up into a variety of level bands. Here's the dungeons he named, and their suggested level ranges:

  • 1-4, The Deadmines
  • 1-4, Shadowfang Keep
  • 5-10, Blackfathom Deeps
  • 5-10, Scarlet Monastery
  • 11-16, Scarlet Monastery second wing
  • 11-16, Dire Maul
  • 17-20, Azjol Nerub
  • 17-20, Onyxia's Lair

This isn't a single adventure chain, but rather a sequence of locations that you might return to more than once. Bonus Reactions adds some useful context, that you're likely to go through the same location more than once with different objectives.

That brings us to Dire Maul. Crit Hit the Giant gives a helpful deep read for each of the pages of the preview content. There are three key sections. The first and most obvious is a massive keyed map for the dungeon, lightly adapted from the original WoW map. The information for the dungeon is split up into smaller sections, and it looks like they'll correspond to the instanced zones of the WoW original.

In place of NPCs with exclamation marks over their heads, the dungeon has a table of potential plot hooks. Two have been revealed so far: Furgus Warpwood wants you to slay his corrupted kin, Tendris, while Orhan Ogreblade has a new plot to conquer the Stonemaul clan, which involves installing one of the players as their new ruler. As far as I can tell these aren't actual WoW quests that Furgus or Orhan ever gave out, but they sure feel like they could have been.

There's also information for the unique characters you'll find in each subsection of the dungeon. The Warpwood Quarter characters have been revealed, all of them bosses and NPCs you'll have encountered if you've played through the main Dire Maul quests; the runaway Fel Imp Pusillin, Felsworn Satyr Zevrim Thornhoof, and the petrified Old Ironbark. Dialogue-skipping WoW players may discover that there's more backstory here than they realised.

The impression I'm getting is that this will be a playground that does need some effort from the dungeon master to animate - but that's not inherently a bad thing. The major bosses from the most famous WoW quests are in place, and there are some suggested motivations that could bring characters to the zone. But the information so far suggests these dungeons won't be exhaustively-keyed and location-based dungeon, but more like a stage. That should make it easier to tell your own story with them, and port them into other settings, but may leave you having to do more of the work.

Which WoW dungeons do you most want to play through in D&D? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Roguelike city-builder sensation Against the Storm reveals board game adaptation
content:
Indie city-building roguelike Against the Storm is getting a board game. Developer Eremite Games has teamed up with the guys at Mindclash Games to create a co-op eurogame style strategy board game, which promises "deep strategic gameplay" and "high replayability".

In case you clicked but haven't heard of it, Against the Storm is a highly randomized city-builder roguelike, where you build temporary settlements in a fantastical post-apocalyptic world beset by Blight Storms and regularly reclaimed by the wilderness. Our sister site, PCGamesN called it "a near perfect Roguelike strategy game" - high praise indeed!

This will be a cooperative board game for 1-4 players and a press release says it has a mixture of "worker placement, resource management, city-building, exploration, and adventure". A heady concoction, indeed! Just like the video game it's based on, there will be "variable setups with highly randomized resources and a deep economic system that rewards adaptability and long-term planning".

You can also play the game with standalone sessions or as a longer campaign, with the end goal of stopping the storms altogether.

Apparently, Mindclash Games - makers of Trickerion and Anachrony - reached out to Hooded Horse to set up a partnership two years ago. This was because CEO Viktor Péter got hooked by the game and realized Against the Storm - with its deep and complex systems, great sense of progression, and dark but charming atmosphere - had a lot in common with the types of games Mindclash likes to make.

Meanwhile, Eremite calls Mindclash a group of "likeminded creators who prioritize gameplay and respect their community", and in what is really quite a sweet video promoting their partnership, the team's developers say nice things about each other.

In this video, Eremite founder Łukasz Korzanowski praises the board game developer's titles, like Voidfall. Despite being a 'deep, thinky game', Lukasz says that its clever use of iconography meant he rarely had to pick up the manual after reading and understanding it the first time.

"It opened my mind to how frictionless you can make the gameplay with some smart ideas," he says.

According to Eremite, Mindclash "has all the creative freedom it deserves" in creating the game but the finished title will stay true to the world Against the Storm players "know and love".

The game's not coming to crowdfunding until the middle of next year, May 2027, though it does already have a Gamefound where updates shall be posted.

For the latest and greatest board game news, follow Wargamer on Discord!
