title: Commander Focus: Sphinx's Approach, Text-Changing Effects, & Immortus, Master of Eternity
content:
Folks, they got me. I never thought I’d be extolling the virtues of a card ‘you can play any number of copies’ of, but here I am, reporting in after having purchased all pieces necessary for paper aside from those arriving in Reality Fracture. The culprit in question? Sphinx’s Approach, a color-shifted version of Dragon’s Approach appearing at Common in Magic’s newest set. As a bit of background, I tend not to enjoy cards like the Approach—historically, they homogenize your list and tend to have a fairly strict power ceiling, with the best thing they can do being the tutoring of some powerful Creature you’d have preferred to Poly/Scramble into. A lot of the panache of these cards is stripped away when you realize they’re just worse Polymorphs with harder deckbuilding restrictions, and at first glance Sphinx’s Approach appears to be of a similar kind. You’d need your targets to make the fact you can play any number of the card matter, and moreover, want to play more than one potential Poly option in a desired order. A wide enough pool, with a specific tutor chain, and ideally alongside a Commander that supplements the playstyle in a truly unique way. Done, done, and most definitely done. I mentioned it during our review of Marvel Super Heroes, but I’ve had my eye on Immortus, Master of Eternity since he was first previewed, and Sphinx’s Approach not only makes him worth exploring, but vice versa as well. You’ve probably seen that Sphinx of the Chimes does some heinous stuff in a list like this, but let’s talk about the card that pushed me to spring for this list in paper: Exchange of Words.

"A deck can have any number of cards named Sphinx's Approach."

First, though, a bit of background. For a deck based around what I’ll term ‘Basic nonlands’, like Sphinx’s Approach, a few considerations must be made: How many are you playing, to what end, and what can you do to squeeze the most from your remaining limited slots? To answer the first question, we’ve got to jump into the hypergeometric calculator. What a calculator like this does is measure the rate at which you’ll see a given card(s) in a certain number of cards drawn or milled, based on how many like cards that are played in your list; as an example, we need to see 5 copies of Sphinx’s Approach to get the festivities going, and if we play 29 copies, we’ll be able to see 5 or more Approaches in our first 20 cards 75% of the time. If that jumps up to 39 copies, that same 75% chance to see 5+ Approaches exists in our first 15 cards, instead. To that end, most lists playing Basic nonlands settle at around ~35 copies of their chosen build-around, give or take. It’s enough to the extent that you’ll be seeing copies throughout the game, and hit key metrics like an 82% chance to resolve a Ripple trigger successfully from Thrumming Stone (a key card for these strategies). Sphinx’s Approach is different, though, because unlike Dragon’s Approach or Slime Against Humanity, the card itself pushes you to see more copies, by being a double-pip Quick Study. The more Sphinx’s Approaches that you cast, the more likely you are to see additional copies, and so on—this means that, unlike its peers, we’re actually incentivized to cast these Spells rather than just mill or Ripple through a deck stuffed full of redundant pieces.

Appropriate, with JoJo Fridays returning this week.

Enter Immortus. Coming in at 4 mana, he has the ability to tap for {U} equal to the number of cards you’ve drawn in a given turn, with the caveat it can only be spent to cast noncreature Spells. We’ll talk about his Power-Up later, when we start covering win conditions, but suffice to say this gentleman was tailor-made for Sphinx’s Approach. Unlike its peers, the Blue Approach is double-pip, meaning it’s far less easy to cheat on its cost compared to something like Dragon’s Approach. Immortus, however, makes Blue mana. There are also 29-39 cards in your deck which draw cards, and at a rate of 3 mana per 2 cards alongside your draw during the draw step, Immortus at his very worst allows one Sphinx’s Approach to pay for the next. That’s the power floor, and it’s a decent one, but where things get silly is when you’ve drawn 4-8 cards in a given turn, and start playing cards like Cerulean Wisps to repeatedly add more and more mana. Immortus is, between his floor and ceiling (power...room?) a Storm Commander, and a reasonably compelling one! Especially if you have any sort of discount on your Approaches, chaining between draw spells and untap effects can tear through your Library, and get the right pieces in hand to pop off. At his utmost, however, the ceiling of the strategy, Immortus is a win condition. It’s time to talk about the Sphinges we’re Approaching.

Riddle Me This

The three Sphinx cards we’ve included in this deck are not the ones which lead to any sort of deterministic endgame; that is possible, by combining Eligeth, Crossroads Augur, Prognostic Sphinx, & Curator of Mysteries, in order to discard and draw through your entire Library purely via Sphinges. If you play Eligeth in the Command Zone, alongside Kydele, Chosen of Kruphix, you get a more deterministic endgame than with Immortus, in exchange for not adding colored mana. It’s a notable tradeoff, but the real defining factor in my choosing Immortus is the fact that we don’t need to play any bad Sphinx Creatures. Sorry Prognostic Sphinx, but you don’t make the cut. Instead, we’re on the trio of Sphinx of the Chimes, Sphinx of the Second Sun, & Consecrated Sphinx—these three do everything, and each makes a compelling case to be the option you tutor for after resolving your fifth Approach. In order of your usual access chain, let’s start with Chimes: This card has been rightfully hyped for its interaction with the Approach, being able to pitch two and draw 4, effectively shortcutting 6 mana worth of spells. You do of course need two Approaches in hand to make this work, which is where our handy dandy hypergeometric calculator once again comes into play. At our current count of 29 copies, there’s a ~33% chance to draw 2+ Approaches out of our 4 cards, allowing us to continue the chain. On 39, this goes up to ~51%, although Chimes as your sole wincon would want even more. That said, filling your deck with an obnoxious amount of Quick Studys is a recipe for a list you play once and put down, which is why Sphinx of the Chimes is more our means than our end. That brings us to Sphinx #2, Sphinx of the Second Sun: Coming in at a whopping {6}{U}{U}, this behemoth gives us an additional beginning step after our combat step (meaning untap, upkeep, & draw). We’re huge fans of this card for a number of reasons, least of which is the fact that it’s one of the only Sphinges to untap our Commander, usually netting 4+ mana and a card in hand. Crucially, it’s worth reminding ourselves that summoning sickness doesn’t fall off at Upkeep and instead occurs at start of turn, which means Second Sun doesn’t solve all our problems when rebuilding. That mana cost though, it does do something special—our strategy’s core win condition hinges around some niche interactions with Power-Up, and a card from Unfinity that most folks have forgotten about, Exchange of Words.

Draw like an Egyptian.

Exchange is one of only two Commander-legal cards to switch textboxes, and the only one that doesn’t make your opponents tear out their hair. When it enters, similar to an O-Ring effect, you swap the textboxes of two target Creatures for as long as it’s on the battlefield; this can in theory be used to rob opposing Commanders of their text, but we quite like the text on our Creatures. So much so, in fact, that this deck’s primary win condition is swapping the textboxes between our Commander, and Sphinx of the Second Sun. Under the hood, Exchange uses Layer 3, text-changing effects, where each targeted Creature loses their rules text, and gains the others' abilities. Copiable values aren't transferred, it's strictly what's written, and moreover this effect persists even if Exchange itself loses its abilities while on the board. This is all covered in the Unfinity Release Notes, but one thing to keep in mind is that the text boxes aren't literally swapping, but instead that new instances of each target's text overwrite the other's after the trigger resolves. This requires a bit of explanation, when it comes to Power-Up as a mechanic—it’s a deeply odd one, because the ability’s cost reduction fluctuates with the card it appears on, with colored pips beyond the required cost overflowing into the colorless reduction.

I covered this set of interactions in full on a Puzzlebox a week back, but in short, Immortus’ massive {5}{U}{U} Power-Up at best costs {3} on himself, but can cost a cool {0} if possessed by a Creature with a printed mana cost of {5}{U}{U} or higher. Unlike a rule like Emerge, which references mana value, Power-Up is all about mana cost (see CR702.193), which means it's a rare ability that scales with the printed cost of the card it appears on. Go figure, Sphinx of the Second Sun has a cost higher than the price on this Power-Up. While yes, it costs 3 mana to transfer texts by casting Exchange (the same as we’d pay with an Immortus that’d entered in the same turn), given it’s a noncreature Spell we can use Immortus’ mana to pay for it. Moreover, if we were to, say, blink Exchange itself and ‘print’ a new textbox each time it entered, by way of a Displacer Kitten flicker, we would be able to make use of a free Timetwister with every noncreature cast. That in turn leads to Immortus producing 7 more Blue mana per tap, or even more, if we have our final Sphinx onboard: Consecrated Sphinx. I don’t need to tell you Consphinx is good—it’s a Game Changer for a reason—but here it makes our Immortus Power-Up dig through half of our Library at a time. We draw 7, as does each opponent...leading to us drawing an additional 42 cards, for a total of 49. Seeing half our Library at a time means we can start to ‘four horsemen’ Lotus Petal and similar, until we assemble the means to cast Blue Sun’s Zenith 3 times, drawing out each opponent in one go (courtesy of the mana generated by Immortus). It sounds janky, and it’s enabled by way of an Unfinity card that should have perhaps had an acorn stamp, but that’s precisely why it’s cool. There’s absolutely no way this interaction was planned in design, and it’s part of why Immortus is the best Sphinx’s Approach Commander.

Out of Space, Not Time

With the terms of engagement laid out, it now becomes important to talk about the omissions, the cards which didn’t make the cut, but not for lacking of trying. See, in any deck based around a basic nonland, the space not taken up by your buildaround + Lands is far more slim than in other lists, so obvious inclusions like Faerie Mastermind aren’t synergistic enough to be worthwhile, in spite of the fact that they’re objectively good cards. We’re on the bare minimum Sphinx’s Approaches, at 29 out of likely up to 39, and 32 Lands (counting MDFCs). Those are greedy ratios helped only by the fact that Approach itself is a hand smoother, and it leaves us at only 39 cards to form the remainder of the list. The next culling of cards came as a recognition that we’re functionally a Storm deck, therefore couldn’t fit tools to play on opposing turns; Eluge, the Shoreless Sea was a shocking casualty, as it seems fantastic here, but while it normally provides 8+ mana per turn cycle, it only supplies 2-4 per turn. Immortus fills that role, and feels better for what we intend to do, but to be clear Eluge in the Command Zone could make an interesting Approach Commander in its own right. Along similar lines to Eluge, basically all of our interaction fell by the wayside, lacking the Game Changer slots for Cyclonic Rift or the best countermagic, and needing to keep the train rolling in terms of untap effects over tools like An Offer You Can’t Refuse & Misdirection, two cards I desperately wanted to slot in. We’re not a fragile list---there’s a ton of ways to give Immortus or our Sphinges Hexproof—but our gameplan is to compare game pace with opponents, and aim to come out on top, rather than interrupt their gameplans. Faith in our linear path of play is paramount, because the way Approach & Immortus works requires you commit full bore to density on things like untap effects. The only ones we’ve cut are those which don’t provide Hexproof, or are too pricy.

Balancing between untaps and Approaches is a nightmare to manage.

Also not appearing in this list are wheels & self-mill, for the most part. These are normally fantastic inclusions for getting your basic nonlands in the graveyard, but here we have such a slim pool of targets that milling one over too early can be disastrous. There are ways of getting them back in the Library, such as with Conjurer’s Bauble or Immortus’ Power-Up, but these aren’t always accessible when building up our board. The one wheel to make it in is actually Arc of Fortune, by way of the brand-new Variable Chaser—this is a second way to repeatably trigger Displacer Kitten, and the mana produced by Immortus immediately outpaces the cost of recasting the Prepared spell to get our Chaser blinked. It isn’t a win condition, as the wheel is optional, but it’s still a fantastic tool if we don’t have a Sphinx in hand, or are pushing into the lategame. Speaking of win conditions, while not technically a victory in of itself, there was no chance we’d go without Narset, Parter of Veils as one of our Game Changers with a Timetwister-esque effect in the Command Zone (mandatory, no less). It’s highly possible that you get to pass around the table with each opponent having but one card in hand, even if your Storm turn doesn’t go fully to plan. Finally, pour one out for the discounters we aren’t on, including the new Geist of Saint Thalia & Dirgur Focusmage; I tended to find that Immortus produced enough mana, if built around, to outpace the discounts when getting down to brass tacks. The Focusmage gets closest, as playing its prepared Braingeyser over Blue Sun’s Zenith seems like a far more efficient path to victory, but there’s not actually enough 5+ mana Instants & Sorceries we’re interested in to turn it on, during the endgame. Buyback & Splice don’t increase the mana value of their respective cards, so Capsize & Everdream are out, so we’re otherwise down to jamming Misdirection or similar into our own Spells...not exactly compelling. If the restriction on Extra Turns were changed, we could just play Nexus of Fate repeatedly on an empty Library, and never actually take the turns (instead Braingeyser-ing people to death), but that worries me in terms of the letter of the law Bracket-wise. If you’re okay with that, swap BSZ for Dirgur, and find room for Nexus. It’s probably better. Hell, just taking infinite turns and Powering Up each turn passing around the ability does get you infinitely large Sphinges & Immortus, just a thought.

Example Decklist: Immortus Chimes In

One card here that’s worthy of calling out is Energy Tap, because while Exchange of Words is the easiest way to enable Power-Up, we can ultimately force it through at full cost by tapping something like our Sphinx of the Chimes with a few Blue mana spare. These Sphinges' mana values are big, and represent a ton of mana we can funnel into hardcasting one from hand (if stuck there) or cards like Thrumming Stone to get the ball rolling. We can even use Energy Tap as a means to recast Immortus, if he dies and we’ve got a Sphinx up. Great card. I’d also like to highlight Bilbo, Thief in the Night as a cool card here, largely for the fact that he’s just a 2 mana rock which occasionally allows us to ‘Flashback’ a Spell at a discount. You’ll see this often in lists going forward, but if you have a 4 mana Ux Commander you want down early, Bilbo is often better for you than something like a Fellwar Stone. He’s a Blue mana dork that only assists in accelerating your Commander at worst, and at best helps a ton with navigating turns where you need one more Spell that’d otherwise be out of reach.

There are also minor tragedies, with the exclusion of Hour of Eternity & Leyline of Transformation being the most depressing. Hour is a way to funnel Immortus mana into Creatures, and can be a stellar way to access a Displacer Kitten you’d milled over during the course of a game. It’s absent, however, because...Immortus’ Power-Up and enough draw power finds those cards again anyway, with no risk of losing them forever to exile. Leyline would be in here, if we took the Dirgur path, because finding any of our key Creatures via Sphinx’s Approach sounds delicious. There is the mild downside of maybe playing too few Approach to cycle back through them in the midgame, removing 5 from our pool of 29 each time, but it still has some cool applications.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

Playing this at Bracket 3 means you have access to Consecrated Sphinx & Narset, two cards which suit our gameplan so well it’d be impossible to go without. That means we’re kinda barred from Bracket 2, where Sphinx’s Approach is more likely used in lists playing the 50+ copies to execute a Chimes win, or play strictly for value. Immortus can do that, sure, but having additional colors is likely worth more when you lack Game Changers. The better question is whether this list can play in Bracket 4, and that’s similarly tough to justify. Quick Study is not a cEDH playable card, even at fringe, and B4 approaches that format in terms of game pace. Sphinx’s Approach is a perfect candidate for Bracket 3, and does plenty of interesting things in the context of that power level. It’s the Goldilocks zone for decks like this.

Putting the 'X' in Sphinges

Harry Conway's promo for Approach is magnificent, and tracking down enough copies is going to be quite the quest.

Immortus has beaten out Monk Gyatso for me as the fastest turnaround between a deck’s concept and its acquisition in paper. Of course, I don’t yet own 29 copies of Sphinx’s Approach, but I’ll be attending the prerelease(s) to snap up any errant copies that show themselves. I’m beyond hyped to get this shown off at LGSes and conventions I attend, least of all for the fact that it’s a Sphinx’s Approach deck. At the outset of Reality Fracture, I expect to see a few of these crop up in my circles, led by such options as The Ur-Sphinx or some discounter, but as is the case with basic nonland strategies, these tend to get culled for being too janky or too linear; each of the options for these cards which require a third of your deck space have a preferred Commander they tend to stick to, after the novelty wears off. For Dragon’s Approach, it’s Florian, and for Persistent Petitioners it’s very obviously Bruvac. I’m confident enough in my testing to make the bold assertion that Immortus is in the company of those illustrious peers, the best option for Sphinx’s Approach decks.

These are still the early days of the card though, and indeed the archetype as a whole. Heck, for the first few hours following the card’s reveal, I had planned out a Kydele/Eligeth version of this article—that ended up performing far worse in testing, and with fewer interesting interactions, hence it being a footnote in our coverage of Immortus. This wasn’t going to be a paper deck for me, however, until around 3:30am the night of the preview, when I was searching for ways to make Blue mana, having found that to be the limiting reagent in Approach. I’d been looking to build something with Immortus at the helm, and even talked about him briefly in the Power-Up Puzzlebox; I had that mechanic on the mind, and then checked the mana values of some prospective Sphinges to tutor out...and then intended to sacrifice Immortus and plant him under Agatha’s Soul Cauldron. Then Quicksilver Elemental. It took some heinous Scryfall syntax to finally reveal Exchange of Words to me as an option (having pretended the only relevant card from Unfinity was Saw in Half), but at that revelation I knew this list was destined for greatness. I’m shrewd about what I bring to paper, with the last one having been Gau, Feral Youth this past April. At time of writing, Immortus has <150 decks. I expect that to change, and fast.

Until next time, don’t forget to go back in time to defeat your morally unscrupulous earlier self.

title: Tabletop Battles Goes to the London Grand Tournament! (Conquest: Last Argument of Kings)
content:
Each year the biggest Conquest event in the UK takes place at the London Grand Tournament, held at the end of September. It’s a fantastic event with people travelling all over the UK (and some even coming in from overseas!) to enjoy 5 games of Conquest. Players arrive with all ranges of experience and competitive aspirations, from brand new to very experienced.  If you can only make one Conquest event a year, we really recommend this one!

Unfortunately Para Bellum’s community team have been unable to join us this year, due to the event conflicting with the Conquest World Championships in Chios. Nevertheless, the UK Vanguard team (thanks Elliot!) is running the event with Para Bellum providing extra prize support.

As the LGT is often one of the biggest events in the Worlds season, it can often be decisive in determining who will represent our region next year, and many players will spend weeks or months preparing their list. Others will only just decide their faction in time for list submission! With a handful of us from Tabletop Battles attending, we’ll share some of our thoughts building up to the main event of the tournament year.

DanDaBossman, Deadly Trout and General Cross in theme for LGT 2025!

General Cross

With the small life change of parenthood this year, Conquest has been firmly on the backburner this year with my attendance only made possible a couple of weeks prior to the event. I’m happy to be able to attend once again, the people in the community are always the best reason to come along. I’ll once again be rocking my W’adrhun as neither of my other armies are assembled yet…

That being said, I can’t quite put down my inner competitive streak. Having two 4-1 and one 3-2 results, I’m hoping that I can still place well even with the lack of practice by faction experience and a little rust-removal with a few practice games. After taking 4th place last year with my W’adrhun “Warburton’s Wholemeal” list (so named for my four units of Warbred!), I don’t think I want to stray too far into more experimental ideas that I’ll be figuring out on the fly.

I’ve been torn between the classic Speakers list of Hunting Pack, Quatl and Thunder Riders, a well known competitive staple, or an updated version of the Warburtons Wholemeal list after the point changes last year. I’ve not had enough experience with Chieftain led Tribes to run it well, or had the time to try some of the newer infantry ideas out there using the Scions, despite both doing well in other events.

In the end I felt that the Speakers list would struggle into some of the more ranged-heavy lists like Sorcerer Kings, Weaver Courts and Dweghom so I’m going to run a revised version of my Scion of War list. Everything in the list hits hard and can stick around just a bit longer than expected thanks to the Tenacious and Hardened once-per-game supremacy. Now just need to see if I can get any more paint on this lot before the event…

So, what’s the game plan? Why the list? Well…The most important and practical reason is that it's painted. I’ve been wargaming for about fifteen years. This is the first army that’s been fully painted. If I go down, I’m doing it in style! #SWAG. Last year’s list was what I had to hand from two starter boxes. My collection has grown since then, mostly on sprue (don’t judge me!), so we’re adding some new friends into the mix.

Thorakites were a staple last year due to being Light scoring regiments. That got removed and they dropped off my radar for a while in favor of less Lights, more Hoplites and maybe just a Selinoi unit. Recently I brought them back with a Polemarch each, Andromachos and an assortment of gubbins. In games recently, including Derby tournaments and the legendary Cows vs Dinosaurs, run by our own General Cross, they have performed quite well and have been scary. Five Cleave 3 Flurry attacks followed by the rest of the unit can put out a world of hurt. The Aristia and Alloys, coupled with Fluid formation, makes them very maneuverable.

Hephy is always a must for Cleave 3. He does a lot of the hephy lifting ;) [Editor: Ugh.]. Arguments can be made for Thyreans but I’ve found they are glass cannons and need to be used carefully. Hephy also gives a little bit of Interference which is always nice.

Hoplite blocks give that sweet, sweet Defence 4, and provided you’re not being flanked (Rule One of City States: don’t get flanked!) will be a solid road block to most enemy units. Unless they’re Varangians. Damn Varangians, they ruined Varangia!

New additions include the mighty Talos, for more Defence 4 goodness, Fearless and Resolve 4. Cleave 1 is ok in a pinch but his job is to plant his feet and brace for impact. Next is a single chariot for those infamous City States drive bys. Sadly I only have two and the other isn’t painted. Finally new for LGT is the Companion Cavalry. They were very useful in previous tournaments but usually needed an Ipparchos which is too expensive for what he offers, and they’re also more glass cannony than Thyreans which is saying something. 

Polemarch warlord means some flexibility in using his “I go first this round” supremacy and being able to choose between Polemarch Alpha and Polemarch Beta really helps with that flexibility. Aristarch is here to buff the Hoplites and being the slot slave to bring a chariot and Comp Cav.

Overall the list is a hammer and (D)anvil with strong defence blocks. Hopefully we can make our enemies take it in the rear flank, as is the Greek way.

Sam Isaacson (not Josh) 

The LGT is my personal highlight in the Conquest calendar. I've been to every one, and my performance is nothing if not consistent. 

I've entirely failed to make it to the podium so far, but have entirely succeeded in landing mid table. For someone who tends to lose virtually every game at our weekly get-togethers this is extreme overachievement for me! 

The reason it's always the highlight is the fact that those who turn up to participate, in my experience, are wonderful human beings who are determined to give everyone a brilliant weekend. I love it. 

My plan this year, therefore, is to take the opponent by surprise. Everyone there will have played Conquest a bunch and will have an answer for everything I can bring to the table. So I started thinking about what I could bring that they wouldn't have seen before…

Earlier in the year I experimented with an army list for The Spires that was only two regiments. My conclusion after running it was that two is probably too few, but it's far from being a gimmick. I've stretched myself to four regiments for the LGT.

I like bugs. 

Those of you may remember me from other bug related articles so this should come as no surprise. After a good year and a half of my beloved OD and ghosts I took to this new year with a pipe dream of being the bestest bug in Britain. Since then, I have taken only the Weavers to events and that’s not stopping now! Having braved the month of the first release and being the worst army in the game, to the lovely place we are in now has been a rollercoaster, but one I’ve enjoyed riding. I love the speedy and mobility of the faction and the variety of… who am I kidding, I just love the moths! The first purchase I made and a staple in my lists for the year they’ve been available is a nice big block of moths, ready to drop rocks (Pollen? A smaller moth?) onto unsuspecting heads! 

Hitting my second LGT I’m hoping my borderline obsession with the bugs gives me an edge this year. Coming almost perfectly midboard last year with OD and a 3-2 record I’m hoping to get the 4-1 this time around. I like my list, having a good mix of units rather than just spamming or two, but I feel this gives me options vs all opponents which I like. Also, I like variation and it looks pretty. The dragon is holding on to its place solely on how much effort went into painting and getting it to stand upright on its damn base!

I’m still a little concerned about facing other ranged heavy armies, or the magic dominance of SK as, despite the high defence and wound bugs, I have a lot of rather squishy units too, but only time will tell now. The addition of the Gallowglass has really helped vs armour, which was previously my biggest bug bear, but I do have to be very careful to ensure they deal the damage needed before they get focused down. 

For my season I went with spring, I find the extra speed very helpful the turns it pops, and I love the heal bloom effect that comes with it. Don’t be fooled by my winter snowy bases, that’s just the knock on effects from global warming. Yes, the tree-bug army player likes the environment, how shocking ;)

title: D&D's Lord of the Rings spinoff takes an unexpected journey to Gondor, Rohan, and 5.5e
content:
RPG publisher Free League has launched a new crowdfunder for its two Middle-earth systems, The One Ring and The Lord of the Rings 5e. The new Backerkit campaign promises three new books for each game. One travels to Rohan and Gondor, while another offers a bestiary of classic creatures. Lastly, there's a new, standalone core rulebook for each system - which means we're finally getting Lord of the Rings in D&D 5.5e.

"The revised The Lord of the Rings Roleplaying 5E Core Rules updates the game to the 5.5 ruleset and makes it fully standalone", says a press release from September 22. We saw a pretty hefty overhaul of DnD classes and DnD races in the 5.5e changeover, so it'll be interesting to see how Free League has adapted its Middle-earth character options.

The One Ring's rules update sounds more marginal, but there are some substantial promises. Apparently, "the updated The One Ring Core Rules reorganizes and clarifies the rules, refines character creation and advancement, and revises combat, with new cover art by Antonio De Luca".

Additionally, both versions of the game include Strider Mode, a solo variant that was previously only available digitally. Free League also swears that previous material for both games remains compatible with these updated rules. Plus, "existing owners of either core rules manual on Free League Unbound or DriveThruRPG will automatically receive the revised digital version once completed."

As for what's new new, we have The White Tower and the Hall of Gold, and Realms of the South. The former is for The One Ring, and the latter is for D&D. Each sourcebook "takes takes players from Minas Tirith and the fiefs of Gondor to Rohan's great halls and open plains".

New locations, campaign frameworks, adventure hooks, and character options are found within. We can also expect additional rules for mounted combat and travel by boat.

Lastly, we have our bestiaries: Creatures Strange and Foul for TOR and Of Orcs and Evil Things for D&D. Each book "brings together adversaries ranging from Black Númenórean spies and Haradrim champions to the Nine Ringwraiths and their winged steeds". These books also officially bring Ents, Woses, Balrogs, Dragons, Ollphaunts, and other Nameless Things to the systems, with new and updated stat blocks.

The Backerkit campaign offers exclusive collector's editions of all books. Plus, backers pledging before September 24 receive a free bonus art print of their choice. Shipping is forecast for 2027.

Want to chat more about D&D or Lord of the Rings? We're exceptionally nerdy about both in the Wargamer Discord. Let us take you on a very unexpected journey.

title: MTG sphinx card spikes by staggering 1,100% after Reality Fracture spoilers
content:
Multiple MTG sphinx cards are spiking in price right now, after Reality Fracture's spoiler season has drawn to a close. The most impressive spike is for Unesh, Criosphinx Sovereign, which - according to the tracking tools on MTGGoldfish - has seen a meteoric rise from just $1.20 to $15.20 in just one week. That's a jump of 1100%, so hats off to anybody who picked up a ton of these a month ago. Lunch is on you.

The reason there's so much hype around Magic: The Gathering's sphinxes right now is because the creature type gets special treatment in Reality Fracture. There are six strong sphinx cards at rare or mythic rare in the main set, but more importantly the Ur-Sphinx brings back the busted eminence ability, encouraging thousands of Commander fans to try out this tribe for the first time.

The Ur-Sphinx has an Esper color identity, allowing you to include all the best sphinx cards in your deck. And it has an equivalent to the Ur-Dragon's eminence power, making all sphinxes cheaper just for being in the command zone. You don't even have to ever play the Ur-Sphinx (though it also has a powerful card stealing ability that looks mighty fun) to make it a viable leader for a sphinx typal deck.

While dragons are a much more supported tribe than sphinxes, the novelty factor is huge here. Suddenly there's a reason to go out and buy all the best sphinx cards, when there never was before, and the creature type as a whole has become much more valuable off the back of all the hype.

Unsurprisingly, the biggest mover Unesh, Criosphinx Sovereign is probably the most valuable card you can put in an Ur-Sphinx deck - not for its useful card draw ability, but for the fact that it reduces the cost of your other sphinxes by two mana. See, there aren't a lot of low-cost sphinxes in Magic. We're looking at five, six, seven mana for many of the best cards in this faction.

If you can reduce that by three instead of one, you're suddenly at a point where you can plop down multiple very powerful creatures in a single turn. And that's a pretty good place to be.

As well as Unesh, another great sphinx that's seen a spike is Sphinx Ambassador, up from $20 to $50. This is a really fun card with just a single printing (in Magic 2010). When you deal combat damage with it, it triggers a fun mini-game. You search for and select a (creature) card from your opponent's deck, and if they can't guess what it is, you get to play it for free. That's really cool and has some neat synergy with the Ur-Sphinx's card-stealing ability. More importantly, it's a pretty strong, and old sphinx card that has only ever been printed once.

title: Turn Order: What Is Cyberpunk Red, and Why Should You Play It?
content:
The Cyberpunk universe is suddenly everywhere at the moment, be it the video game, the Edgerunners anime, or the many spin-offs and crossovers those media have spawned.  But this is Tabletop Battles, so maybe you're aware that all of this stuff actually originates from an RPG of the same name.  That RPG had a big re-release just a few years ago, and is still going strong with regular updates and content, including some recent additions based upon the aforementioned spin-offs.  It’s also really good.  So, what’s it all about and why should you give this game a go?  Well just slot this chip, choom, and let the braindance begin.

History of the RPG

Cyberpunk 2020 cover art, from R Talsorian games

The original Cyberpunk RPG was released by R Talsorian games way back in 1988, mere years after the term itself had been coined to describe a new wave of science fiction exploring themes of high tech and alternate culture.  The game’s designer, Mike Pondsmith, was heavily influenced by the novel Hardwired by Walter John Williams, amongst other now-familiar staples of the genre such as the film Blade Runner.  Shortly afterward a second edition followed, titled Cyberpunk 2020, which for most fans became the definitive version of the game, and still retains an avid player base.

A third edition of the game was released in 2005, using a completely different game system, but was so negatively received that it is officially non-canonical.  Let's move on!

Cyberpunk Red was released in 2020, still under original creator Mike Pondsmith's auspices, and offered not only an evolution of the much loved 2020 rules, but also an expanded future timeline with a somewhat grittier vision, bringing the game into a new near-future of 2045.

The Cyberpunk Universe

Cyberpunk red Night City 2045 cover art, from R Talsorian games

Most people have their own idea of what cyberpunk means, but as far as the universe of the RPG is concerned, this is a world in which international political entities have lost much of their power to mega-corporations.  The gap between the richest and poorest in society has reached new extremes, with those on the corporate paycheck receiving all the benefits of modern living and privatised services, while those at the bottom of society live in run-down and lawless urban hells at the mercy of street gangs.

Alongside these economic and political developments, technology has massively accelerated in certain areas, most notably cybertechnology and biotechnology.  The human body is modifiable and changeable to an almost limitless degree.  Artificial eyes, limbs, and internal organs are commonplace, as much for fashion and an edge on the mean streets as for any medical need. 

Finally there is the Net.  In Cyberpunk Red the Net has fallen from its days of a global internet of the kind we all know and enjoy, as an onslaught of terrifying killer AI programs necessitated its fragmentation into LANs protected by advanced AI firewalls.  But for those with the right skills, hacking is still one of the best ways to get data, money, and control.  Just don’t get yourself killed by Black ICE.

Cyberpunk has its own geographical epicentre of these themes, the most extreme example of all things Cyberpunk: Night City.  While nominally part of the fragmented near-future USA, Night City is a de facto independent state, ruled by a convoluted city council composed of private and public interests, and free of many of the national laws and taxes.  A sprawling megalopolis, Night City is home to unnamed millions and a rare few who somehow emerge from the teeming masses.

So what about the player characters?  The PC’s are Edgerunners, guns-for-hire who make their living in the cracks and shadows of society, taking the work too dirty and dangerous for others, living for money and fame, for as long as they can.  Whether you’re a street kid with big dreams, an ex-corp with a grudge, or just someone with a unique skill who stumbled their way into the life, you know the only things that matter in this world are your rep, your edge, and The Rules:

  • Attitude is everything
  • Style over substance
  • Live on the edge

How Does It Play?

Interior art from the Cyberpunk Red rulebook, from R Talsorian games

Basic Mechanics

Cyberpunk Red is a relatively simple game, with the vast majority of actions performed with a simple D10 skill check.  Each character has a set of attributes, and a set of skills, and ranks in both are combined with a D10 roll in an attempt to beat a Difficulty Value, or DV, which might be a specific number defined in the rules, or a value set by the GM to reflect the relative difficulty of a task.  If the action is directly opposed by an NPC, e.g attempting to persuade them to do something, or trying to hit them in melee combat, then the GM makes a roll using the NPC’s skills, and the required DV for the PC to beat becomes the GM’s roll.  This is a very intuitive and effective catch-all system that is easy to pick up quickly.  The only other dice you’ll need are a few D6, for rolling damage in combat.

Characters and Roles

In Cyberpunk, the player’s class or archetype is called their Role, and there are ten to chose from.  These include Cyberpunk’s equivalent of the fighter, the Solo; its bard, the Rockerboy; and the likes of Techs, Netrunners, Fixers, and others whose particular skills make them an asset in the near-future underworld they inhabit.

There are multiple methods for generating characters' stats and skills, from simple plug-and-play options to complete custom builds, so GM’s and players can work this out as they please.  A core part of character creation is the PC’s Lifepath.  This is a summary of the character’s family background and journey to the point of becoming an Edgerunner.  It is a really important part of the player’s role in brining their character to life, and an invaluable tool for the GM to get hooks for personalising in-game stories for the player.

The final piece of each Role’s kit is their Role Ability.  This is a single powerful skill that encapsulates the character’s mastery of their field.  The Solo for example, has multiple different combat benefits that they can activate and switch between at any time.  The Rockerboy can convert NPC’s into fans and then exploit their fandom.  The Nomad can call on customised or exotic vehicles as and when needed.

As a result of their kits, characters in Red are very much good at the things they are supposed to be.  The Solo can easily dispatch a gang of goons or security on their own; the Fixer can source improbable and scarce items (or find someone who knows how to get them); the Netrunner can compromise a secure network and disable its security systems, and the Rockerboy can charm the pants off whatever they set their desires on.  This tends to lead to feel-good situations for players, who can live out their character fantasy and contribute in the way they expect.

Combat

Red’s combat mechanics are mostly quick and simple, with only certain specialisations having a lot of mechanical depth.  Initiative is rolled once at the beginning of combat and then persists through it, and PC’s with high Reflex stat or Solo abilities will normally go first.  Combat rounds are three seconds long, and players may make two actions, a move, and then some other kind of interaction, be it making an attack of some kind, or operating a device, etc.  There are plenty of tactical nuances to combat, such as earlier-acting players able to hold actions (“I’m going to aim down this corridor and shoot the first thing that appears”) and PC’s and NPC’s alike having access to combat abilities that can limit other actions, such as suppressive fire that forces combatants to take cover.

Most weapons can be fired once or twice in an attack, and do damage in the 2d6 to 4d6 range. If two or more 6’s are rolled, a critical injury is caused, which does additional damage and an additional random effect, including extreme results like blowing limbs off.   Armor worn by players and NPC’s reduces the amount of damage taken, and is quite strong, with the starting armor given to PC’s able to shrug off the worst of a lot of small arms fire.  And taking cover is very effective, with shoot-and-move tactics making mobility a significant asset.  As a result, Red leans toward spike damage as the most impactful part of combat.  When players or NPC’s cause critical damage, combats can swing suddenly and dramatically.

Melee combat has some of the greatest options, with the Martial Arts skill having a wealth of unique style-based abilities that can really dominate action economy, while Brawling has powerful grappling attacks that can immobilise and restrict other combatants.  Most melee attacks ignore significant parts of armor protection, making them feel relatively powerful.  Meanwhile, the Evasion skill can be very powerful in avoiding all manner of attacks, with players who are built right able to ‘bullet dodge’ multiple attacks against all but very lucky NPC’s.  This ability is so good that it is often house-ruled to tone it down a bit.

Advancement

The primary method of advancement in Cyberpunk Red is via Improvement points, which are awarded in chunks after a session or adventure is completed.  They reflect a combination of task success, roleplaying, and team-work between the PC’s.  Characters can chose to invest the Improvement Points they have gained from each session into either individual skills (the lower they are the easier they are to improve) or to raise their Role Ability.  The latter is where the real power improvements are generally found, with increases improving not just their mechanical aptitude but their status as an exponent of their craft.  Players who attain the higher Role ranks are on their way to being legends, with abilities that let them call on favours from public personages, play gigs to stadiums full of people, or make news stories around the country.  But Red has relatively slow advancement, and reaching such dizzy heights will take a long time.

Gear-wise, players can find many ways to get hold of better guns and armour, and to customise and upgrade them.  A Fixer can source you military-grade gear through the black market, while the Tech Role's Maker ability lets them modify and invent equipment to create powerful new gear, working with the GM to come up with new stat lines and abilities.   The other option is cyberware, which can provide large power spikes by pumping PC's raw stats or by granting new abilities.  Fancy inbuilt nightvision?  A monofilament whip built into your finger?  Bullet-proof plating under your skin?  Skill chips that allow you to become a moderate practitioner of any art?  The possibilities are enormous, but come at the potential cost of Humanity.

Humanity is Red’s mechanical expression of the mental health and outlook of the player.  It starts at the same level as the player’s Empathy stat, and is modified (usually downward) by various kinds of trauma that the PC experiences.  By far the most common and significant impact on Humanity comes from installing elective cyberware.  The bigger the installation, the bigger the loss, and when Humanity reaches very low levels, PC’s can suffer from the psychological and dissociative effects of having discarded their meat body for power.  Players can offset this problem by paying for therapy in their downtime, but it can be a tricky balancing act to manage.  Humanity can be a bit of a contentious subject among Cyberpunk players, with many feeling that it is a bit of black-and-white system in relation to the nuanced subjects of mental health and self-perception.  I think the Edgerunners anime did a fantastic job of showing how this creeping erosion of self can work in practice, but unquestionably, Humanity exists in Red not least as a mechanical check on simply chroming your way to easy power.

Supplements and Expansions

Cyberpunk Red Edgerunners mission kit art, from R Talsorian games

Red has had a steady stream of updates since its release, including monthly DLC via the R Talsorian website.  Most of this content has been collected and re-released with other new material in the Interface Red books, which are now up to Volume 5.  These are great places to start to expand your game world, as they are full of new gear, settings, and expanded mechanics.  That said, I think you might find some content more or less interesting or relevant for your own campaigns, so I would suggest checking out what’s in each book before you buy.

In addition to this, there have been several full supplements, including most recently the most comprehensive look at Cyberpunk’s flagship location, Night City 2045.  If you want to run your campaign in Nighty City, this and the Danger Gal Dossier, which includes detailed guides to the most significant gangs and power-brokers of the city, have you covered.  The best expansion for adding new gear and cyberware to your game is Black Chrome, which has everything from monofilament katanas to cyberpets, and food processors to attack helicopters.  For the anime and video game fans, there is the Edgerunners Mission Kit, which is a very slick expansion that provides rules for new technology and campaign play in the 2077 era.  Most notably this includes rules for quickhacking, which gives Netrunners the ability to hack opponents in combat.  Finally, Single Player Mode gives you all the tools to run Red solo, though many of its random tables and 'quick & dirty' rules (Netrunning in particular) will be of great interest and use to all GM’s.

Why Should You Play It?

Cover art from the Cyberpunk red worldbook, from R Talsorian games

A unique, incredibly immersive world, and a lightweight, evocative rules system are two huge reasons why Cyberpunk Red is an easy recommendation.  Cyberpunk also offers players the chance to play characters on the greyer end of the moral spectrum.  No one has to act the hero here.  You can indulge your impulses and excesses, and enjoy dealing with the consequences too.  I’ve had multiple PC’s in my games become addicted to drugs, as well as suffering the dehumanising psychological effects of excessive cyberware modification.  These aspects of the game make playing a campaign in Red so much fun, with your character development about much more than just pumping stats.

Fundamentally, Cyberpunk Red has a powerful focus on roleplaying and immersing yourself in its world, rather than its mechanics.  Players are encouraged to try cool stuff, act like badasses, and aim to be legends.  Social skills and interactions with NPC’s are every bit as important as combat skills (I’ve run plenty of cyberpunk adventures where not a shot has been fired) and in the huge open world of the near-future, players are limited only by their imagination (and maybe the odd dice roll) in how they solve the problems you throw at them.

For the GM, Cyberpunk is a game that works really well for one-shots and intro games.  Structuring an individual session as a single task, job, or heist that the players have been paid to complete very much fits the theme of the game world.   It also works well with player groups who change from session to session, as each group of Edgerunners can be assembled afresh by a Fixer for each new job.  And as player progression is not linear, groups of mixed experience can play together perfectly well.

The Cyberpunk universe is such a unique and fun world, and Cyberpunk Red does a great job of bringing it to life and making it easy to enjoy, so I heartily recommend it to all wannabe Night City legends.

title: Metal legends Sabaton and Wind Rose pledge their support to the Warhammer World Team Championship
content:
The medieval city of Talavera de la Reina, east of Madrid in central Spain, will soon play host to one of the nerdiest metal gigs this century. On Monday, metal legends Sabaton, Wind Rose - they of Diggy Diggy Hole fame - and power metal band Nanowar of Steel, announced that they will be playing shows in the town from October 25-27 to coincide with the Warhammer: the Old World World Team Championships, with each band declaring its support for one national team.

From speaking to fans of the game I'm pretty sure that the Warhammer community has adopted Sabaton - with its high energy and aggressive power metal and recurring theme of historical warfare - as its unofficial soundtrack, and it seems that the regard is mutual. The band has declared its support for its home country, Team Sweden, in the upcoming tournament.

Both Wind Rose and Nanowar of Steel are Italian, and Nanowar of Steel has called shotgun on Team Italy. Wind Rose has thrown its weight behind Team England, stating "yes we are Italian and we love our country, but the English are playing an army of Dwarves… and no Dwarf must be left behind!"

For metal heads unfamiliar with the tangled history of Warhammer games, Warhammer: the Old World is the classic flavor of Warhammer, with Orcs, Elves, and Chaos Warriors marching in big square regiments to fight over a fantasy world that is shaped a lot like our own but is populated by rather more dragons and daemons. The game was removed from sale in 2015 and was missing for almost a decade, but Games Workshop relaunched it at the start of 2024 and it's been hugely successful since.

The World Team Championships is a fan-organised tournament with 160 players from 20 teams all across the world, with an admittedly heavy bias towards European and Anglophone nations. When two nations face off, they'll start the round by alternately putting forward players, letting the other team decide their opponents. This creates an intricate metagame; teams must decide which of the many Old World factions their players will field, how to optimize those armies, and then how to pair up players to account for strengths and weaknesses of each army to try and ensure the team as a whole wins the round.

Which metal bands do you think give the most Warhammer energy? I have two whole articles on this, one with bands that aren't explicitly referencing Warhammer, and one with bands that absolutely are (and yes, Bolt Thrower is on there) - but I'm always keen to hear more suggestions. Let me know in the Wargamer Discord community!

Thoughts

I knew it! I knew Imperial Agents were Actually Playable now. I wasn't crazy!

Running Imperialis Fleet as Reconnaissance whips, because their deal is that they can be everywhere, all the time, and have sticky enough units and enough morale and movement tricks that it's hard to stop them scoring. Veiled Blade can only help with this, as it makes the Assassins both good and hard to pin down, keeping the points rolling. Finally, Kroyle helps shore up the list's weakness by letting it grind out some foes, though it can still be overwhelmed by some games.

On that front, the opposition here is a mixed blessing. On the one hand, the Take and Hold game is definitely one that this list wants to play - it is ideally placed to guarantee scoring quarters every turn, making its path to 100 pretty even unless killed fast. The bad news is that the Custodes absolutely are one of the builds that can just full send and try and overwhelm the fleet forces.

I think two things likely determine the outcome here. The first is that the Agents having gone extra transport-heavy is really good for them, as it both adds mobility and slows down the clock of how fast the Custodes can kill them. The other ace they have are the various Inquisitor and Agents squads, which provide lots of Devastating Wounds (suitable for using out of oa Firing Deck to boot) and a few big shots, upping the chance of killing enough of the Custodes forces for them to clain victory.

That doesn't mean it's a sure thing, because the Allarus in particular will give as good as they get here - their grenades into all these squishy Character units are a nightmare. There's only the two squads though, so if the Agents prioritise taking a chunk out of one with Draxus popping off, that might hamstring the golden host hard enough for them to win. There's also the curveball of using Tome Skull battle-shocks and hoping. If you're the Custodes, you'd definitely like the third Allarus unit here, especially as that would provide an option to split one squad to respond to whatever the Agents get up to. As it was - the fleet sailed to victory!

title: 40K Weekend Update: The Lion Takes a Points Hike, Orks Bully Events
content:
Hello Dear Reader, welcome to a new column we're going to be publishing weekly here at Tabletop Battles! We've wanted to do something a little faster and more topical for a while now around 40k events, and this week we're kicking things off by talking about the major goings on of the weekend for 40k - what's happening with events and news in the space.

What about Competitive Innovations? Great question - we're still doing Comp Innovations. This article is for news hot off the presses and headlines, not deep dives into lists. If you want the quick hits on a Monday morning about the weekend's events, this is where we'll cover those. It won't always be me doing coverage

Speaking of which, we have some big news to start with this week, so let's go ahead and get things rolling:

The Lion. Credit: Jack Hunter

Games Workshop Corrects the Points on the Lion, Deathwatch Terminators

Maybe you saw Liam's unhinged rant about the Lion in our review of Codex: Space Marines and the Dark Angels Datasheets. Mabye you saw David Gaylard's YouTube video going off on the new datasheet and how the design of the Lion was absolutely insane. Either way, Games Workshop heard our collective concern and adjustments have been made. We were notified this morning that the points for both Lion El'Jonson and Deathwatch Terminators have changed. Specifically:

  • Lion El'Johnson will be 415 points on launch, not 335
  • Deathwatch Terminators will be 190 points for 5 and 380 points for 10

This is a big change, and much-needed. The Lion may still be a problem after all this - it's always hard to tell how things will play when you give a 16-wound model a 3+ invulnerable save and a 4+ feel no pain against mortals and psychic attacks - but it's at least going to actually cost you something to bring this guy. Is the Lion the new Defiler? Yeah, probably. But at least we've got a reasonable cost for him coming out of the gate.

For the Deathwatch Terminators, this is also welcome, but we suspect we're just hitting the tip of the iceberg on Deathwatch changes. Although conceptually cool as hell, the Deathwatch support Detachment really opens up a massive can of worms when you combine it with Codex: Space Marines, and the ability to combine those units with standard leaders creates some truly crazy combos.

Bad Moons Flash Gitz. Credit: Corrode

Orks Dominate the Weekend Results with 18% of TiWP Spots as Codex: Orks Hits Events

Codex: Orks properly hit the ground running this past weekend, and players were ready for it. The faction jumped from 2 event wins and 8% of TiWP (Tournaments in Winning Position Percentage) last weekend to a whopping 18% this weekend, snagging three event wins with 4 undefeated players. Next closest were Necrons at 13% and Leagues of Votann at 10%.

The most interesting part of this is that there isn't one single way to run the faction to success; Wrecaks seem to be the most common shared Detachment among the lot, though Shoota Boyz, Blitz Brigade, Dread Mob, Runt Swarm, Flyboyz, and Bully Boyz were all part of the undefeated lists over the past weekend. That speaks to both a versatile army with lots of play and a number of potential problems to solve from a balance standpoint.

Over the weekend, Orks averaged a 60.7% win rate, second most of the weekend behind Deathwatch at 61.3%. No other faction even came close to that rate - Space Wolves were next at 57.5% - though it remains to be seen if this is a fluke or not. The Deathwatch numbers are almost certainly an anomaly, given only six players played the faciton, but we recorded 46 Ork lists at GT+ events, making that a much more stable result.

A Quiet Weekend Between Challengers and LVO

It was a relatively quiet week this past weekend, with 11 GT or higher level singles events - a welcome break for Wings and Tom Lowman after the breakneck pace in recent weeks. We're in the usual lull between NOVA/Challengers Cup and the upcoming Las Vegas Open now, and the upcoming release of Codex: Space Marines figures to represent a tectonic shift for the game moving forward. Our biggest tracked event of the weekend was Münsterland Major 5 in Rheine, Germany, a 91-player, 5-round GT won by Jasper Lange running Leagues of Votann.

Credit: Warp Speed Distribution

Dumpster Fire Wins Studs and Snotlings in Ontario

Of course, this was just singles - There were also 24 Teams events we tracked this past weekend, including Studs and Snotlings in Kitchener, Ontario - a 208 player, 8-man teams event with 5 rounds run by Warp Speed Distrubition. Studs and Snotlings was won by the American team Dumpster Fire, who defeated Nasty Gamers in the final round to take home the gold. Congratulations to Ari C, Austin Warfel, Ben Greenlay, Ben Rubenstein, Dan Meloro, Jeremy Borg, Sarah Ivankovic, and TJ Lanigan - plus Coach Nick Warburton - for their win.

You can find the Wargames Live stream of the event here.

Games Workshop Shows of New Custodes in Their Fall Preview

GW's big fall preview showed off a few interesting things - Nobz and Legion of the Damned in Kill Team do matter for 40k players - but the big release we're going to be talking about for 40k is the Adeptus Custodes. In addition to showing off new Terminators in the WarCom preview article, their video also showed off the new statlines, revealing that even the most basic Custodian Guard will be monsters who move 8", with T7, 5 wounds, Ld 5+, and OC 3. The good(?) news is that they'll only come in units of 3 models, so we suspect we're entering a new age where Custodes armies will look more like War Dogs armies in terms of model counts, just being made up of a bunch of Space Marine captains. Their damage output also figures to be increased.

That wraps up this week's news but if you like the format or if there's something you think we should cover in future recaps, let us know - we're happy to make adjustments!

title: Neglected in the big Warhammer preview, Lord of the Rings gets grizzly new Orcs, and updated Battle Companies
content:
One major Games Workshop game was missing from the Warhammer Big Autumn Preview show last Friday: the Middle-Earth Strategy Battle Game was conspicuously absent. But as if to offer fans of The Lord of the Rings a consolation prize, this Monday the firm revealed an updated multipart plastic kit for the vicious Mordor Orcs, which will be the centerpiece of a new Battlehost army box set.

The old monopose Mordor Orcs models have been in service since 2003, so this is a most welcome refresh. The new kit will build 24 Orcs, just like the old kit, but this time they're multipart, giving you at least some cosmetic choice over how you equip them, and perhaps some gameplay flexibility.

The Warhammer Community article announcing the models states that sixteen of the models will be equipped with hand weapon and shield, with eight shield designs and eight hand weapons including swords, picks, and maces - GW doesn't mention it, but looking at the pictures it seems that a couple of these Orcs can be built with bows. The other eight can then be equipped with two-handed weapons or spears.

As well as a standalone box set, this kit will be available in a new Mordor Battlehost army set. The Orcs are accompanied by six rather Warg Riders - plastic kits that are old enough to drink - and the relatively recent model for the Witch King of Angmar, mounted and on foot.

If you're not aligned with the forces of evil, you may be pleased to hear that a new edition of the Battle Companies supplement has also been announced. This campaign mode is all about developing the story of your troops over multiple battles, collecting gold and influence for your successes while racking up injuries and fatalities.

Do you have plans to march for Mordor? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Five things D&D underdark adventures should borrow from real world caverns
content:
Down into the depths, under stone and over stone, the road wends away through cavern and cave, away from the light, into the Underdark. Adventures in the subterranean world of the Underdark are some of the most evocative in Dungeons and Dragons - and lessons from real life cave exploration can help make your party's lightless adventures feel even more real and gripping.

The ideas here all come from a trip to Blue John Cavern, a tourist attraction in the UK's Peak District which is still a site of low intensity gemstone mining. Descending the narrow steps into this awe inspiring cave system, it was impossible not to imagine how the different D&D classes might respond to such an environment.

Air and rock

Caves are created by magma forcing its way up from below, water drilling its way down from above, and other geological forces or fantastical magic - they're the children of violent ruptures in solid stone. Nothing about them is uniform. If a cavern has a flat floor, the players should ask "who leveled this out, and why?"

Caves are as likely to run vertically as horizontally, with the adjoining tunnel mouths sometimes great distances above or below the nearest flat ground. The lower portion of a cave might be a single large bowl, but the rock above it could be carved into multiple narrow channels that branch apart like a star, making spider-climbing creatures almost as mobile as ones that can fly.

Water and stone

Caves might provide shelter from the worst of the rain, but this doesn't mean they're bone dry. Water that permeates rock will flow through caves and deep caverns on its way to the aquifer, falling in waterfalls, dripping from ceilings, sweating down rockfaces, and gathering in pools. Heavy rains on the surface can suddenly flood tunnels.

Water shapes the landscape of the underdark: flowstone, stalagmites, and stalactites are all formed by the gradual deposition of calcite as it's leached from the rocks, and where these features show up, the stone is likely to be slippery underfoot.

Light and life

While caves are isolated from the surface world, they're not hermetically sealed, and surface plants and creatures will find their ways inside. If they don't find their way out, that usually spells their doom - but the presence of electric lights allows moss and algae to gradually colonize rock faces. In the magical Underdark, glowing fungi and perpetual light spells could have far more impact, creating pockets where the flora and fauna of the surface mingles with that of the underdark.

Indelible Marks

Flowstone has a surprising property - touching it with bare skin subtly discolors it, and rock that's frequently touched eventually changes from a natural white to a sickly brown-yellow. In the Underdark, discolored flowstone is a sign that a route sees frequent use - and different D&D races may leave different marks. A band of discoloration high up on a stalagmite could be a sign that ettins and ogres regularly pass through, while deep purple stains might indicate a route frequented by the Drow.

History of Use

If sentient creatures occupy a cave system they invariably rework it to suit their needs, leaving traces of their presence after they mov on. That could include steps cut into stone that follow the route into a mine, or pulley systems left in vertical shafts that once brought supplies down and treasure back up. Natural springs are likely to be dammed and directed into convenient troughs to provide clean drinking water.

In the Underdark, sentient creatures are as likely to enter a cavern from below as from above, and they're likely to make their own peculiar accommodations. Azers might unstopper magma plugs to provide light and heat; Aboleths will use magic to flood chambers that enable them to progress upwards; Beholders will widen out vertical faults to allow them to conveniently float up and down through their domain.

Has a natural wonder ever inspired you for your D&D home game? What surprising features of caves have we missed out that we should have mentioned? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Typhoon rains off major Pokémon tournament
content:
"Inclement weather" caused the cancellation of a major Pokémon TCG tournament in Japan today, as Typhoon Dujuan hit in the midst of a national holiday. 80 mph winds batter the country, the Japanese government has issued flood and landslide warnings, and millions have been evacuated from the worst affected areas. Also, the Champions League Pokémon tournament held in Yokohama won't be going ahead today.

Only the September 21 event was cancelled, however - it still took place on September 20 and is expected to commence tomorrow, on September 22 with the main 'Masters' tournament. However, The Pokémon Company warns that "severe weather and disruptions to public transportation are expected on the day of the event", asking "all participants to check the latest weather and traffic information regularly and to prioritize safety when traveling and making decisions."

Champions League tournaments are regional competitions in Japan which, while not as prestigious as Worlds, nonetheless draw impressive crowds, with thousands of attendees. Typically there are three Champions League events each season, with the most successful players qualifying for the Pokémon Japan Championships, the country's next stepping stone on the road to Worlds.

The next Champions League kicks off in Chiba on November 22, and those with priority entry for Yokohama on September 21 will have this carried across to the Chiba contest.

Typhoon Dujuan is the 25th powerful storm to have affected Japan this year. The region is experiencing worse weather conditions than normal, due to the "super El Niño" event.

After Gen Con 2026 was hit by a tornado, it's really starting to seem like Big Wind has it out for us tabletop gamers. Stay safe out there, everyone.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.
